speechtext: What terms of reference are laid down by the government to co-ordinate information and assistance to the unemployed between Manpower counsellors and UIC skilled, trained interviewers?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: CO-ORDINATION OF INFORMATION BETWEEN MANPOWER COUNSELLORS AND UIC INTERVIEWERS
speechtext: When unemployed workers make application for unemployment insurance benefits, they are referred to a Canada Manpower Centre if they require the services provided by the Centre and have not contacted it prior to applying for benefit. Subsequently, if the Unemployment Insurance Commission interviewers determine that claimants who have not recently contacted a Centre are in need of the services provided by the Centres, appointments are made for the claimants to be interviewed by Manpower Counsellors. Also, Canada Manpower Centres provide Unemployment Insurance Commission interviewers with current labour market information. Canada Manpower Centres and Unemployment Insurance Commission offices provide the public with pamphlets, application forms and other material dealing with the programs and services of the other organization. A committee of officials of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Manpower and Immigration has recently been established to investigate further means of co-ordination between the two organizations to provide greater assistance to the unemployed.

speechtext: Does the Canadian government intend to allow or does it allow British soldiers to train in Canada for later fighting in Ireland and, if so, in what manner does the government consider it possible to remain neutral in the conflict between the United Kingdom and Ireland?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRAINING OF BRITISH SOLDIERS IN CANADA FOR FIGHTING IN IRELAND
speechtext:
Members of the British Armed Forces have trained in Canada on a relatively small scale for the past ten years. In August 1971, an Agreement was signed between the Governments of Canada and of the United Kingdom covering this existing training and providing for increased use of Canadian military training facilities by British soldiers. Under the terms of the Agreement, Brit-
April 17, 1972

ish training in Canada will involve a range of activities from flying instruction to training in the use of tank guns, artillery and anti-tank weapons. This training is carried out by the British forces within the context of their NATO obligations, and is not designed to enhance their capabilities in support of the civilian authority in Northern Ireland. The Canadian Government has, of course, no control over the subsequent assignment of these or any other British forces outside Canada. This program of training should be viewed in the context of Canadian and British membership in NATO as a part of a long-standing tradition of bilateral co-operation in the defence field.

1.	How long has Canada been a member of the International Civil Aviation Organization and what are the obligations of membership?
2.	How many countries belong to the International Civil Aviation Organization and are individual countries bound by the recommendations of the majority of the membership?
3.	Has the ICAO made any recommendations about skyjacking and, if so, what are they?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1. The International Civil Aviation Organization, located in Montreal, was created by the Convention on International Civil Aviation (the Chicago Convention of 1944) which was signed by Canada on December 7, 1944. ICAO officially came into existence on April 4, 1947, with Canada as a charter member. The aims and objectives of ICAO are to develop the principles and techniques of international air navigation and to foster the planning and development of international air transport so as to: (a) ensure the safe and orderly growth of international civil aviation throughout the world; (b) encourage the arts of aircraft design and operation for peaceful purposes; (c) encourage the development of airways, airports and air navigation facilities for international civil aviation; (d) meet the needs of the peoples of the world for safe, regular, efficient and economical air transport; (e) prevent economic waste caused by unreasonable competition; (f) ensure that the rights of contracting states are fully respected and that every contracting state has a fair opportunity to operate international airlines; (g) avoid discrimination between contracting states; (h) promote safety of flight in international air navigation; (i) promote generally the development of all aspects of international civil aeronautics.
Membership in ICAO obligates states to comply with the provisions of the Convention on International Civil Aviation. Members are also obliged to finance the operation of the Organization through annual assessments; Canada's 1972 assessment is $US278,959.29. Canada, as host government, also underwrites a substantial part of the costs of the space rented for the ICAO Headquarters Building. ICAO has decided to move into new premises in Montreal in late 1973 or early 1974 and the Canadian Government has agreed to make an annual grant of $1.1 million towards the cost of renting this building.
2. One hundred and twenty-two countries are members of ICAO.
There is no mechanism for ensuring that member states adhere to the recommendations of the ICAO Assembly

April 17, 1972

(all member states) or the ICAO Council (27 member states). Last April the United States of America and Canada co-sponsored a draft convention providing for the enforcement of international legal obligations relating to unlawful interference with civil aviation but the ICAO Assembly transferred this proposal to its inactive list of subjects because of opposition from a number of member states.
3. ICAO has been actively involved with the question of skyjacking and other related matters affecting the safety of international civil aviation for some time. Under ICAO auspices the Convention on Offences and Certain Other Acts Committed on Board Aircraft was signed in Tokyo on September 14, 1963. Canada ratified this convention on November 7, 1969. The Convention came into effect on December 4, 1969.
The Seventeenth Session (Extraordinary) of the ICAO Assembly, held in Montreal from July 16 to 30, 1970, had for its agenda the single item calling for the "development of adequate security specifications and practices, for application by ICAO States in international civil aviation, aimed at the protection of air passengers, civil aviation personnel and civil aircraft by (a) preventing criminal action of any kind that may endanger the safety of air transport and (b) consideration of arrangements under which those responsible for criminal actions endangering civil air transport can be brought to justice." Two Diplomatic Conferences on matters related to skyjacking followed which resulted in: (a) the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Seizure of Aircraft signed at The Hague on December 16, 1970; (b) the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts against the Safety of Civil Aviation signed at Montreal on September 23, 1971. Canada will ratify The Hague and Montreal Conventions as soon as Parliament approves the necessary amendments to the Criminal Code tabled recently in the House of Commons. Neither of these conventions have beeen ratified by the required number of countries to have it come into effect.
The ICAO Council has also set up a Committee on Unlawful Interference with International Civil Aviation and its Facilities to deal with problems of (1) unalwful seizure of aircraft and (2) sabotage or armed attack directed against aircraft used in international air transport or ground facilities used by international air transport. Canada is not a member of this committee.

speechtext:
The hon. member for York South has given the Chair due notice of his intention to request leave to move a motion to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing the specific matter stated by him.
There is little doubt that the matter stated by the hon. member is important and of current concern to Canadians and, of course, to members of the House. At the same time, it is suggested that the matter has been raised on a number of occasions during the course of the current session. The hon. gentleman will recall, for example, that he posed a question on it in the sitting of February 21 last. Since that time the same difficulty has been raised in the House in various other ways. For example, on March 16

the matter was discussed during the adjournment proceedings on the initiative of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, and a reply was given by the Secretary of State.
It may be that in due course it will be necessary or desirable to have the House debate the question of this dispute, but it does seem to me that a motion under Standing Order 26 is not, at this moment, a suitable vehicle for such a debate. As this problem has been pending for a period of several months, it does not appear to meet the provisions of Standing Order 26 which requires that a matter proposed for discussion must relate to a genuine emergency calling for immediate and urgent consideration. It might be added that when determining whether a matter shall have urgent consideration Mr. Speaker shall have regard to the probability of the matter being brought before the House within reasonable time by other means.
The decision I make at this time that the motion cannot be granted does not preclude the matter being brought forward again under Standing Order 26 at a later date. I am just making a procedural ruling to the effect that in my estimation the motion at this time does not meet all the requirements of Standing Order 26.

speechtext:
Orders of the day.
April 17, 1972

Canada Laoour Code

The House resumed, from Thursday, April 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. O'Connell that Bill C-183, to amend the Canada Labour Code, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the context of the industrial unrest which prevails in certain sectors in Canada today, and in view of the fact that there is likely some involvement as far as the government itself is concerned-we do not yet know what stage negotiations have reached as between the government and its own employees in resolving difficulties which have always been a fruitful source of strikes in the past, and in the past few years particularly-it is very important that we give this bill searching examination.
Most hon. members of this House, if they listen to their own constituents, will be aware that there is great anxiety in Canada today with regard to the state of labour-management relations, and the fact that we Canadians, as a people, have been victims over the past several years of unnecessary losses, of unnecessary strife, of unnecessary suffering. It must be remembered that the worker is not the only person to be implicated when there is labour strife. Nor is it only the management in the particular sector concerned which may have to suffer loss and inconvenience. At the present time, it seems that certain individuals, when conducting the activities of organized labour, feel they can extend their deadly pall over all concerned and even beyond. Their attitude is: to hell with the public.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
This has been the case all too often. If I used their language it would be much more colourful and earthy. This seems to be the impression.
I am not assessing blame to one side or the other in any particular industrial dispute. Some portion of blame undoubtedly can be attributed to unenlightened management. Some of it is attributable to the leaders of organized labour, particularly to unofficial leaders. In presenting the bill the other day, the minister said the government was asserting its proper role as representing the public interest in the relationship between organized labour and management. These are fine words, but I honestly do not believe the bill actually carries out the intention which has been implied. I have grave reservations. The minister said:
Our economic performance in the world is of vital importance to all Canadians and it will increasingly be so as the world's economic environment drastically changes through the rest of this decade and, indeed, the rest of this century.
I am reading from the first column of page 1269 of Hansard under date March 29. The minister continued: Good industrial relations will play a vital part in our economic performance and, accordingly, they will be the concern not only of the parties immediately involved but of all the Canadian public. It is with these thoughts in mind, Mr. Speaker, that we have approached the amendments to part V of the Canada Labour Code.
Again, I have some very grave reservations whether the government has actually recognized its role or the purpose, the ultimate objective, of these changes to the Canada Labour Code. It must be remembered that every member of the House must ensure that legislation in the field of industrial relations should promote industrial peace and not lead to a widening of conflict, or areas of conflict, between management and labour. Certainly, it must not lead to a complete or a greater abandonment of the public interest than now exists.
As Canadians, we face a great challenge from many sides in the world today. We have seen declining trade figures in this first quarter with Japan, Britain and the European Common Market, with some very substantial decreases. True, we have had an increase in trade with the United States, but this is only the accentuation of a problem that we have faced for a long time, one that should have highlighted the discussions between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the President of the United States.
One of our biggest problems has been too great a reliance on trade with the United States. If we in this parliament give ill-considered study to the proposals contained in this bill and as a result there is greater industrial strife, then Canada might as well shut shop. Because industrial strife, whatever may be its cause, leads to loss of production, higher costs and more imports. If the Canadian public finds its domestic sources of supply are arrested, then it may well have to buy from abroad, and quite often at higher cost. Some people seem to think that, as in the old days, fleas and bedbugs are a necessary adjunct to man. So, they think that we must have a certain amount of industrial strife each and every year. I deny that this is necessary, Mr. Speaker. This is why I say we must approach this particular bill from the point of view of ensuring that it promotes greater industrial peace than heretofore.
This bill covers only about half a million workers who come under federal jurisdiction, a long way from the bulk of Canada's labour force. But this does not mean that the bill is in any way diminished in importance, not at all. The Canada Labour Code, as the government so claims, should be in the vanguard. It is like a flagship that shows the objective towards which provincial administrations should strive. There are many areas in which labour legislation passed by this parliament has shown the way for the provinces. If this is to be the case, then let us make sure that this bill is one that people can point to as an example of a measure that will promote greater industrial peace.
It is in that light that we must examine the bill. It must not be a bill that results in an indiscriminate abandonment of jurisdiction. The bill must not be merely Pilate-like, that is one who washes his hands of the thing and lets

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
management and organized labour fight it out; that it is a bill that will give each more opportunity to get at the other's throat. I say that that is not the purpose of the bill and must never be its purpose. Therefore, I propose to consider the bill with this particular point of view in mind.
However, if I may say so, Mr. Speaker, we in Canada at both the provincial and federal levels have achieved a certain degree of support from the public generally for social legislation and at no inconsiderable cost. In fact, the cost has been fantastic. One of the budgetary problems of this administration, of its predecessor and of many of the provincial administrations, is that they all face escalating costs for some of the social welfare programs that are on the statute books.
I think that in many areas we in Canada have been too precipitate; we have gone too fast for our ability to pay. Whether through taxes at the municipal level in the form of higher education costs, whether through certain forms of taxation at the provincial level which enter into cost of production, or whether through income tax at the federal level, we have taken far too much out of the Canadian economy at the present time. We have weakened the base of the economy in order to support those programs that ultimately we want to have. We seem to be content, and in many instances more than content, to pile on costs, making our goods less competitive, not only abroad but at home. In some cases costs are unnaturally high. As in the forestry industry and in certain other sectors, taxes and the take of government have now gone up to 80 per cent of net operating revenues. And we ask these industries to be competitive internationally! We ask them to support, in addition, all the programs that we have on our statute books. It is simply impossible, Mr. Speaker, to do so. If by this legislation we impose further costs upon industry, then we will be making those industries even less competitive than they are now. The legislation then becomes self-defeating. To the extent that defective legislation is the cause of the elimination of just employment to any one Canadian, it is deficient legislation. That is what I am afraid of in respect of certain sections of this bill.
This bill does nothing for the protection of the public interest as such. When is it to be deemed that an industrial dispute has reached the point where the public interest is suffering? This bill does not cover the Public Service, for instance. If we look at the extent of the jurisdiction of the Canada Labour Standards Code, we find that the following industries are covered: rail, air, road and water transportation; services incidental to water transportation; interprovincial pipeline operations; telephone and cable communications; radio and television; grain elevators and grain milling; banking; hotels; uranium mining and federal Crown corporations, involving in all about 530,000 workers.
The Public Service itself is covered by the Public Service Staff Relations Act, and is excluded from the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. I should have thought that, having decided the Public Service of Canada will be granted much the same rights as organized labour elsewhere, they too would be brought under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and where appropriate would be subject to that jurisdiction. Certainly, I should have

thought the government would take this opportunity to give itself the necessary tools to deal with the public interest, regardless of the source of the industrial strife.
We know there are many Crown corporations such as Air Canada, for instance, in which there have been a number of debilitating strikes that have caused great loss and great public inconvenience. As a result of the chaos created by numerous unions having labour agreements finish at different times, the whole operation can be undermined and the public interest is absolutely secondary in the consideration of those people who have the dispute in hand. It seems to me that this is and has been quite wrong.
I know there are difficulties in respect of split jurisdictions, and I do not mean by that, joint jurisdictions. For example, what happens if there is a total breakdown in industrial relations of the steel industry and the public interest is being adversely affected? What action could then be taken? I have no ready answer but this is something which might be arranged with the provinces in order to see that strikes do not hold the Canadian public to ransom, because all too often that is the ultimate result. In the case of those strikes against the public sector by the employees of any Crown corporation, and we have had a lot of them, it is the Canadian public that is being held to ransom. It is not management, in the conventional sense, that is being held up, ana it is not the shareholders or directors who are hoping to operate a concern at a profit for private benefit; it is the Canadian public at whose head the gun is being held.
If there is any loss as a result of the strike of CBC employees, it is John Q. Public who will have to absorb that loss. If Air Canada suffers a loss, it is John Q. Public who pays. If the CNR suffers a loss as a result of a long and disastrous labour dispute, it is John Q. Public who has to suffer and pay. So, there is no question that there is greater reluctance to strike ultimately against a publicly owned as against a privately owned operation. In my opinion anybody who, as an advocate of nationalization for the sake of achieving greater industrial peace, says this is the case, is going completely against the record.
I wonder why this bill did not provide for some sort of alternative, and in this regard I have to be very careful of my grammar. I wonder why there was not some sort of alternative to that which we now have. It seems to me there should have been provision for a mandatory cooling-off period. Once there has been a breakdown in the normal course of negotiations, and conciliation and mediation have failed, assuming a work stoppage were to be against the general public interest, then in so far as those industries affected by the Canada Labour (Standards) Code are concerned, the executive should have the power to issue a directive declaring the work stoppage in that industry to be against the public interest.
At that time a mandatory cooling-off period of somewhere between 80 and 120 days could be called for during which the parties must resume negotiations and arrive at a satisfactory settlement. This could be some form of mandatory mediation or conciliation, but the answer must come within that definition. Other countries use labour courts, but what is a decision of a labour court other than the mandatory laying down of the terms of the labour
April 17, 1972

agreements? These exist in many countries in the world. In this country, people have shied away from any question of compulsory arbitration. They do not like it, but many other countries have resorted to some form of this as an ultimate sanction by the public.
When the public of Canada, whose interests are paramount, say "That is enough; there must be a settlement", all we have is some sort of ad hoc solution whereby, if the government feels there is an adverse effect on public interest, it will call parliament into session. What has parliament done under the circumstances? The parliament of 1958 or 1959 had to deal with a strike by the employees of the west coast ferries. What was done then but the invoking of a compulsory cooling-off period during which the parties were directed to renegotiate? Certain minimum terms were established by the legislation. But the parties on either side were under no illusion that on the date specified in the bill-and the same thing applied with respect to the Canadian National Railways I believe in 1964 or 1965-there would be a settlement, and if there were no settlement it would be at the peril of the party disagreeing. That is the force of the public interest.
Therefore, I say it is unfortunate that in this bill there is not a provision to obviate the necessity to call in parliament and involve, shall we say, partisan political considerations. The machinery should exist whereby a mandatory cooling-off period could be imposed in appropriate cases. I will admit that in this area most provincial governments have jurisdiction, but in those circumstances this bill could be some sort of a flagship. I know organized labour does not like the legislation in some of the provinces because it goes too far in another way, but it would seem to me that if there were a reasonable course laid out in this bill there could be a rallying to that reasonable point and an example could be shown to other administrations. Much of what the government has done with this bill has resulted in leaving a great void. It has abdicated its responsibility, as I say, in failing to provide for that option. I would be the first person to approve if someone could think of a better or more reasonable alternative. I would welcome it. I say, however, that one must never neglect the public interest as is now being done.
There is another area in which I think this bill is deficient. Here, I am very conscious of the rights as well as the responsibilities of both sides and the experience we in Canada have had over several years. I would say one of the chief reasons there have been excesses on the side of management and excesses on the side of organized labour is the fact that unions are not legal entities. Unions, unfortunately, in order to redress wrongs the members experienced, because they could not sue, have had to resort to other action. After all, they will not remain inactive. If we read any responsible newspaper that comes out of Montreal we know that on the picket lines at the present time there is violence; there are actions which would otherwise be illegal. There are wrongs being perpetrated against the public and against other honest, law abiding and innocent employees. This is all done under the mantle of an industrial dispute. Damage is done, injury is perpetrated and there is no recourse under the Criminal Code. Recourse under the Criminal Code is not
Canada Labour Code
the answer. We limit the remedies under the Criminal Code.
All too often after an industrial dispute has been settled, one of the terms of the settlement is that there shall not be any prosecutions or if any charges have been laid that they shall be dropped. But if striking employees in an industrial dispute enter the plant or property of owners with whom they have a dispute and damage or destroy property, why should they be above the law? If I enter my neighbour's property and vandalize it, even though I may have a quarrel with him, have I the right to say that because I had a quarrel, an honest dispute, I should be able to inflict these damages on him? Of course, that would be wrong. Yet, in industrial disputes sometimes hundreds of thousands of dollars of damage may be done in a spirit of vengeance, in a spirit of coercion, sometimes by hired thugs and goons. Then, I say such actions should not be above the law nor should it be possible to circumvent the law in respect of that sort of thing.
In the same way if management hires thugs and goons to coerce and victimize its employees with whom it has a dispute then the bargaining unit, the union itself, should be able to sue the owners. But today this cannot be done. It must be the individual who takes action. What chance would one lone worker, two workers or even three workers have to establish a case? What funds would they have with which to fight the case? If the union were a legal entity it could take action on behalf of its members who had been victimized. It seems to me by refusing to recognize a bargaining unit as a legal entity, we have forced both sides to take other courses of action which are not as acceptable as a proper proceeding through a court. It is for that reason I believe there is a serious deficiency in this bill. I do not take this position because I feel if organized unions were legal entities they could be the subject of pot-shots or persecution through the courts. This is not the case any more. It may have been in the days when they were fledgling organizations unable to take care of themselves. Perhaps then they would have been disseminated by the strength of owners dragging them through the courts, but that is not the case today. It seems that far too much reliance has to be placed on other courses of action in order to clear up some of the difficulties that arise as a result of an industrial dispute.
There is another matter on which I think this bill is deficient. The previous minister discussed this with me, and I was hopeful he would include it in the legislation. At least there was some hope and encouragement offered. However, I fail to see it in this particular bill. To that extent, I am sorry, I think the government is again showing a lack of leadership in this particular range. After all, the way has in part been blazed, and I say in part only, by the government of Ontario in its industrial relations legislation. I refer to my bill C-48. Frankly, this bill is popularly known as charity versus closed shop union dues. There are people in this country who have bona fide religious principles which preclude them from paying dues to unions organized in the way they are today. If an individual is working for a concern which has entered into a closed shop or union shop agreement whereby there is a compulsory check-off of union dues, that person, having

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
bona fide religious views which prohibit in conscience that person from belonging to such a group, it should be possible for that person to have an amount equivalent to the union dues deducted from his periodic pay and paid to a charity that is recognized by both the union and the individual, a recognized public charity.
There have been cases in Ontario, and I must say they are to my knowledge limited to Ontario, whereby long term employees in some concerns that have become unionized have been discharged by order of the Ontario Labour Relations Board because of refusal to pay union dues but offering to pay an equal sum to a charity. That was prior to the present Ontario act and, I must say, the present act is far from perfect. It only went part way. However, can there be any justification whatsoever for an individual who has been employed or is qualified to take employment being prohibited, because of his religious views from taking that employment?
We have all sorts of legislation starting from the Bill of Rights down through the piece which states there shall be no discrimination as a result of religious beliefs, yet we have this situation as a result of our industrial codes. This bill does not prohibit it. I think these legislative guarantees are a hollow mockery because, as a result of the demands of the big unions, the individual worker is denied the freedom of his religious beliefs. They say you can believe what you want, but because of your beliefs you cannot work at this particular plant or concern. I suppose the next thing we might have might be a denial of the right to work because of an individual's political beliefs. The shoe would then be on the other foot. There would be screaming to high heaven about denials of the fundamental rights of the individual, yet in the labour code we fail to provide safeguards for those rights.
I say it is totally wrong to victimize those individuals of recognized faiths in this country which object to this sort of thing. But any individual should not be allowed to say casually that he does not believe in this type of organization and that it is against his religion. The proof must be there. Yet all we now say to these objectors is that they can work somewhere else. They do not have to work for that particular concern. I am sorry that the minister or the government did not have the political courage to include such a provision in the bill.
In my bill I do not advocate that an individual have the right to pocket the $5, $10, $15 or $20 per month which he would normally pay in union dues. The dues may be less, but there are many who pay $10 or $15 a month. There would be a transfer to a recognized charity. Surely, to the extent the charities are supported by the people making such a stand, the unions could consider this a valuable contribution to public charity in this country. They are not that poor. What I find even more fundamentally wrong is that this is a back door denial of the freedom of religious belief.

speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I also thank hon. members. I will not transgress upon their generosity. I will soon bring my remarks to an end.
There is one point in the bill which I find very satisfactory. No doubt there are others. I refer to the change in the composition of the Canada Labour Relations Board. I have objected many times to the composition of conciliation boards and other bodies of a similar type set up to resolve a dispute. The board is usually composed of a representative of one side, a representative of the other side, and a neutral chairman. In 90 per cent of the cases, unless there is unanimity, the judgment that finally comes down is that of the chairman because the other representatives of management and organized labour have vested interests and will not cross that very definite line down the middle.
I have been engaged in this sort of thing under industrial contracts. Many of my colleagues who practice law and with whom I was associated before entering parliament have told me the same story. They said they were appointed with instructions. They were responsible to their clients. Quite often the representative of a particular bargaining unit was some individual from another union, and also had a vested interest. We never got really worthwhile settlements. I am glad to see that the Canadian Labour Relations Board from now on will be composed of individuals who have an intimate knowledge of, or a particular ability to sit in judgment on these matters. They will be independent of any vested interest. This, hopefully is a great step forward.
I fully agreed on this point with the brief of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. I foresee two difficulties. The first is with respect to the extension of bargaining rights to employees who have supervisory duties over other employees. It seems to me that supervision is a managerial function. If there is to be an extension of bargaining rights to supervisory employees, surely this should not be a matter of legislation but of collective bargaining?
The second point I wish to make is in connection with the provision that a representation unit may get certification on the basis of 35 per cent of the membership initially voting favourably on a representation application, not 50 per cent of the totality of the membership, but decertification must be approved by the majority of the membership of a union.
Other hon. members have spoken about the difficulties arising out of the provisions with regard to technological changes. We know that Bill C-183 is much different from Bill C-253. I hope that at committee stage amendments will be accepted that have the purpose of promoting industrial peace, and that will not afford further opportunities for industrial strife. Bill C-253 had provisions that were rife with opportunities for disputes and strikes. I do not know what it would have contributed to industrial peace in Canada.
I have spoken beyond my allotted time, Mr. Speaker. The House has been very kind to allow me to complete my remarks. I hope that most hon. members of the House will speak at this stage. This is a very important bill. I hope that there will be much interest shown by the public at
April 17, 1972

committee stage, so that we can get the best possible legislation and that when the committee reports back to the House we will have an improved bill. I hope that a way will be found to overcome the matters which I have described as failures. I realize there may be some procedural difficulties, but the government could readily overcome them by taking appropriate action. This is one of the most important bills that we will consider this year. I hope I have approached the debate on it with the appropriate sense of responsibility.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in entering this debate, I speak as one who has been on both sides of the fence. I have spent a good part of my working years as an employee and trade unionist, and for the last 25 years I have had some knowledge of management. Despite the years that I have been associated with management in my own business, I have never forgotten how it feels to be an employee in the shop, and therefore I think I have some perspective in that sense when dealing with a labour bill.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) tended to lose his perspective when making certain comparisons. I was particularly offended by his inference that trade unions and working people were above the law, that they could not be prosecuted because trade unions were not legal entities. I was surprised that he did not know better. All he has to do is pick up any newspaper and he will see that people are prosecuted if they contravene the law in any encounter between labour and management.

speechtext: By whom? Nobody in this country is above the law, neither a trade unionist nor anyone else. It is wrong for the hon. member for Edmonton West to make that kind of inference because it simply does not stand up to the facts.

The charges are dropped by the person who lays them, and not by the hon. member for Edmonton West. It is not his decision to make whether or not the charges are dropped.

speechtext: You have got it so wrong.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
I think it is wrong to come into the House and make charges of that kind which incite people against labour, which distort the role of working people in this country. That is what is wrong.
I was also interested in the hon. member's analogy in trying to equate a trade union with a corporation. Actually, they are reverse situations. Each member of a trade union is accountable and responsible under the law. To say that the association of which he is voluntarily a member must also be responsible is like saying that if a member of parliament commits a crime inside this House or outside it, then the House of Commons is responsible.
Canada Labour Code
A trade union is not a corporation. It is a group of people who have voluntarily banded together to look after their interests and pursue their objectives. In many cases, people in trade unions are elected to the offices they hold. They are not like corporation officers. Is this worse than a corporation that hides behind its charter, and whose officers say, "We have no responsibility; pick up whatever assets you like."? Today, most corporations have limited liability. You cannot touch the members of a corporation, and in most cases you cannot touch its assets beyond a certain definite amount. Yet, we have agreed to that situation. We have said that limited liability is necessary in our society. We do not throw people in debtors' prisons, as used to happen; we now have the procedure of bankruptcy for discharging debt. We recognize in each instance that there has to be some idea of what the liability of the particular group may be. Each group is different and it is not fair for the hon. member for Edmonton West to make a comparison between a corporation, which is one thing, and a trade union, which is something else. I know this is done continuously when even a cursory examination would show that they are different things.
Let me suggest something else to the hon. member regarding the way society looks at rights. If a person owns a factory and has capital in it, he has absolute rights under the law. Within the law he may do whatever he chooses with that factory. He can walk in one day and shut it down, throwing a thousand people out of work. The law allows him to do that because it is his money that is invested and he is free to do with it whatever he wishes. The havoc that may be created by the shutdown is not his responsibility, according to the law. The man who has worked there for 30 or 40 years giving his loyalty, his energy and brains to the work of that shop has no rights, beyond two months' notice of lay-off in some provinces. Labour has no rights in the eyes of that kind of law. We are still living in a society that says that property has ultimate rights and labour has virtually no rights.
I am surprised that my hon. friend would niggle about the minor rights being conferred upon labour in this bill, and the fact that the Parliament of Canada is moving to redress some of the differences that exist between the rights of ownership and the rights of labour. It is a philosophical question I admit, but a very important one to the man who works in the shop. He has a real sense of grievance if he is thrown out of work after perhaps 30 years of service. Sure, the company has paid him, perhaps even been good to him, but he has worked hard too and the company has not suffered through him. They made a bargain and both worked out the arrangements, but if the company decides to close down or realize a capital gain or move its operation somewhere else, that man who has worked in that shop all his life has no rights. I say, Mr. Speaker, that any rights this parliament can confer upon him, any sympathy or understanding that this parliament can muster on behalf of the working man, is not misplaced and he is entitled to it.
Like everyone else, I would like to find a resolution, a reconciliation, between absolute individual freedoms and social responsibility. I would like to feel that it is possible to maintain social responsibility while everyone does

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
exactly as he pleases. We know, in fact, that this can only be an objective; we know, in fact, that we have to make some kind of compromise between these two objectives and sometimes we have to give up some of our freedoms in order to ensure social responsibility. In this chamber we have heard many debates in which members argued against one type or another of legislation because it infringed upon the right of the individual either not to pay taxes, not to be part of a program or not to be included in the legislation, yet in so far as the whole of society is concerned, some of those rights are infringed upon every time a piece of legislation is passed. I do not think there is any legislation on the books that does not infringe upon those rights in some way.
I make these remarks in connection with the statement of the hon. member for Edmonton West about people who are members of religious groups and who do not want to pay union dues. I wish there were some way of working that out.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext: We will find a way.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext: Very often these things cannot be worked out. Whether a person belongs to a union or not, in a shop he receives the benefits of membership; he may even receive benefit because there are unions in the area. This confers a social responsibility upon that person to make some kind of contribution to that union.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext: What about religious beliefs?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext: It is very difficult to deal with religious beliefs and I admit that. The situation is not quite as black and white as the hon. member for Edmonton West would have us believe. It is not that a union wants to force anyone in this way. In my conversations with trade union leaders, they indicate that they wish a formula could be found that would be fair to the trade unions, that would bring justice to all and enable them to give a greater measure of freedom to those with religious beliefs. This is assuming that it is a violation of a person's religion to belong to a trade union. We know it is a difficult problem, but to say that unions are terrible because they cannot resolve that problem is to say that parliament itself or all legislative bodies are terrible because they have never been able to resolve that problem either. In fact, we have difficulty in trying to reconcile the problem of individual rights with social responsibility and collective action.
