speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had originally intended to speak on the sections dealing with technological change, but as always it is difficult to follow the hon. member for Edmonton West. It is difficult because he makes such a useful and clear contribution to the debate and difficult because he always manages to say something which antagonizes my sense of fairness.
We have to be very much concerned about industrial peace in this country, Mr. Speaker. We know that very few people benefit from labour strife or strife of any kind. This is not to say that all strife can be eliminated, but certainly where it can be avoided it is important to avoid it. I think one of the best ways of avoiding labour strife would be to incorporate a clause in the labour code that would provide for participation by the worker in the decision making process when technical change is involved. In that sense the bill before us is somewhat worse than the original version, because it permits this matter to be negotiated in the new contract but does not permit the opening of an existing contract for that purpose. I have received a number of letters, as I am sure most hon. members have, which are violently opposed to the inclusion of a technological change provision in the labour code. Many people are far too afraid of the so-called dangers of such changes. I am of the contrary opinion. I think that if you bring the workingman into the picture when you consider making technological change
April 17, 1972

there will be a great deal more labour peace in the country than there has been in the past.
You know, much depends on how one views labour, on the image one has of labour. For some in this country, labour, unfortunately, is some kind of beast that must be restrained and chained. According to those people, any attempt to bring labour into the picture or to rely on the intelligent judgment of labour is bound to meet with failure. If, on the other hand, you feel as I do, that labour is intelligent, concerned, and willing in most cases to reach an agreeable, intelligent settlement based on legitimate positions, you will have a great deal more confidence in the clauses dealing with technological change. This bill is only making suggestions; there are not many improvements in it. What it speaks of is already happening in our society. Therefore, the bill is not breaking new ground. It is not as though management is not consulting with labour. It is my impression, after having visited many plants in my riding, that management recognizes the value of consulting with labour when changes are contemplated. Intelligent management officials have been doing that for a long time. This bill will provide them with additional encouragement. It will encourage others as well to continue the dialogue between management and labour.
The great enemy of the workingman in the plant is fear, fear of the unknown. You must be a workingman to understand that fear. True, the businessman has his own fears, his own problems. He wonders about solvency; and he must compete with others. He has his worries. One tends to forget that the man working in the plant also is beset by worries. He is worried about his job continuing, about being displaced by a machine, about what will happen to him. His worries are genuine. Any effort made by management or by legislatures to allay that fear and bring the two parties together to discuss these problems openly will bring more industrial peace. That, Sir, more than anything, is what is necessary if there is to be true industrial peace in this country. Even if you were to outlaw unions tomorrow and outlaw strikes, there would still be dissent. There is ample evidence to show that there is dissent without unions. There are slowdowns, and things of that kind, where unions do not operate. History shows that unions have brought more industrial peace, rather than less. In countries where strikes are outlawed, there is more industrial strife, more dislocation and more damage to the economy through wildcat strikes, revolts, and disagreements, than has ever been caused through labour-management disputes in countries like Canada where strikes are legal.
Let me talk more about fear, and about how that fear arises. At one time most of the plants in my riding were family owned. Management was paternalistic, that is true. The bosses and the workers went to church together. They knew each other. Sometimes they even came from the same villages in Scotland. Their parents knew each other. The result was that if a man stepped out of line once in a while, if he did not show up for work because of something that happened at his birthday party or at a wedding celebration and he had a big headache on Monday morning and was not perhaps as efficient as he
Canada Labour Code
might have been, his boss understood. The boss knew him. He knew the man was sorry he was late for work. The boss knew the man did not drink all the time and that this happened only once in a while. He knew the man had worked in the plant for 20 years, and that his father had worked in the factory before him. There was understanding and communication there. In a plant like that, there was mutual confidence. After all, the worker could say, "I go to church with Mr. So-and-So and our children know each other. He says hello to me." That relationship meant something, and there was a great deal of security in it. That security has gone today.
Today, the workman does not even know who his boss is. Everything is done on orders from a computer. Computers spill out instructions. The guy on the line is set aside from his foreman; the foreman is set aside from the managers. There is a whole new pecking order, a new hierarchy. The corporation is now a big organization. Corporate bureaucracies have developed. Things are done in triplicate and quadruplicate. It is small wonder that men cling to their rights. The workers think that their rights must be guaranteed on some kind of paper, otherwise they are without protection. Even though the guarantee is written on a piece of paper, the worker does not feel secure, because he does not know just how good the guarantee on paper is. In Canada, the situation is even worse because the boss is away in Milwaukee most of the time, or in Vienna, or in California. Faceless ones run the bureaucracy. They do not know the worker's job. In his work, the worker is a little cog in the whole operation. He does one small part. Nobody really knows what his talents are. He might be a fine machinist, yet on the production line, even though he has been trained as a machinist, he must stand there and punch a press and turn out little parts in large quantities. That is the kind of climate you will find in our factories. True, some plants are still run on the old basis; there is some rapport between labour and management, and the workers retain some sense of identity. For most working people, and I am talking about white collar as well as blue collar workers, that identification has largely gone.
If, because of this bill, management consults with labour on technological change, we shall take a small step back in the direction of understanding between the two parties. We are opening the door to some kind of consultation so that the parties can call on each other for advice and assistance, and so that the workers will know what the future holds. If they do that, that will be all to the good. In cases where this fails to take place, rumours fly and fears are generated. Often those fears are worse than the truth. It is better when there is confidence between the parties. I speak from experience.
I am thinking of two specific occasions that involved workers in my riding. One case involved a shoe factory, and the other, Polymer Corporation. Certain changes were to be made; plants were to be phased out, employees were to be let out because of technological and managerial change, and so on. In both cases management was wise enough to call employees together and explain what was to happen to them, what the position of the company was and why those things had to be done. Management did that before rumours circulated. They tried to make arrangement for the re-employment of affected workers
1360

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
in other parts of the corporation or in other parts of the community. The result was that the people who worked in this plant were sympathetic and understanding rather than hostile. They did not like what was happening, and they could not be expected to like it. But they did understand the situation, and these changes were effected with the minimum amount of friction because management had shown sufficient intelligence to take its work force into its confidence. Had this not been the case, a climate of fear and rumour would have been created in which intelligent discussion would have been impossible.
We tend to forget that North America has led in the field of productivity, that despite difficulties in labour-management relations this has been an enormously productive society. We sometimes forget that labour has not, in fact, opposed change or automation. In many instances, labour has been an ally of management particularly when it has been shown that labour, too, will benefit from changes proposed. Perhaps the most obvious example is the case of the coal workers in the United States under John L. Lewis. An agreement was made providing for the most far-reaching technological changes, even to the extent of contemplating the displacement of a large percentage of the miners. The union in question, whatever its other faults, realized that if its members were to receive decent wages the industry needed to be productive. Management has been able to modernize in North America in a way which has astonished the world. This has been made possible largely with the co-operation of the trade union movement. Why is this always forgotten? Why is it forgotten that the trade union movement in North America has never stood in the way of change? There are examples to the contrary, but usually these have arisen in circumstances where a climate of fear and uncertainty existed. This brings me to my final point.
If any labour legislation is to be effective, if technological change is to be accepted, we must, as a prior condition, provide for full employment. It is difficult to expect a man who is to be replaced by a machine to be sympathetic to that machine or to the rational argument of the engineer if he cannot hope to find a new job to replace the one he has lost. The legislation before us will have its value. It is an improvement. But until we live in a society committed to full employment, all the great legislation which comes before this House, all the changes we are making, will not work-I have said this on other occasions, and I say it again, now; I am sure I speak for every member of my party. Given a policy of full employment, given a policy of reasonableness, of trying to understand the frustration felt by men who make their living in factories, men who do not own the shops but who must depend, now, on the government, because they cannot really depend on their employers to understand them, the legislation is likely to prove its value.
I hope I may be able to convince the hon. member for Edmonton West of the reasonableness of the labour position, and I hope that some of the hysteria created in this country and directed against the labour movement will diminish, that the normal Canadian attitude of fair play will reassert itself. Of late there have been many hysterical outbursts against trade unions. Trade unions are not

perfect, of course. I am close enough to them to say I have seen things with which I do not agree. But by and large, the trade unions are being attacked in a way they do not deserve. In many quarters there has been a lack of sympathy and understanding of the work they are trying to do.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) on his recent appointment? I believe he is a very kind and considerate minister and, like the former minister, is very interested in providing a sound legal framework for the process of free collective bargaining in the federal jurisdiction.
Bill C-183 updates the industrial relations section found in Part V of the Canada Labour Code. Since this Act has been unchanged since 1948, it is not surprising we should be called upon to change our thinking in the field of labour relations. We have not kept pace with the times; workers are not happy with their lot in life because the cost of homes, rents, clothing and groceries, the basic necessities of life, has far outstripped the capacity of weekly take-home pay to meet them. The old idea that one week's pay was sufficient for one month's rent, or one month's mortgage payment, no longer applies in our society. As a result, workers are not able to provide the necessities of life for themselves and their families on one pay cheque.
Our society has failed to provide workers with the type of home they can afford to buy, largely as a result of red tape and regulations of all kinds applying to building construction. Construction companies have not been able to provide the average Canadian with the type of home he can afford. Consequently, he is obliged to pay high rent, making it impossible for him to save the down payment for a new home.
Many years ago, workers were easily satisfied to receive annual wage raises of 5 per cent or 6 per cent because they knew that out of these annual raises money could be set aside for future emergencies or for saving against retirement. Today, though, our society has changed and in the process the worker, the old age pensioner, the war veterans, have been unable to keep pace, largely because most of them are living in quarters whose cost is not in keeping with their take-home pay or monthly pensions. There seem to be no apartments available for rents which the worker can afford to pay while at the same time accumulating the down payment on a home-the down payment is too high, anyway. Thus, the worker feels that although he is employed, he will never be able to get ahead. New industries choose locations outside town and city boundaries in areas not serviced by vast, economical transportation systems. The worker is therefore forced into purchasing a car to take him to work and back. These are the main complaints of workers as they strive to be successful. At every turn their expenses run ahead of their ability to make the necessary money to survive.
I believe in the process of collective bargaining. If both sides bargain in good faith and if the impact of technological change is fully discussed at the bargaining table, there is no reason for strike action. One does not need to be a well educated person to realize that when a worker cannot supply living quarters and the basic needs of his family on the amount left to him from his monthly pay
April 17, 1972

cheque he will be a hard man to satisfy when it comes to negotiating a raise. This is because he feels he is doing no more than working to keep even, that he cannot save toward his future.
For many years labour and district management of federal companies were able to solve many of their grievances on a local level because regular meetings were held to iron out differences of opinion on small issues. Management personnel were men who had come up the hard way; they were interested in the employees and their families and enjoyed watching the men progress in our society. To me, this was collective bargaining at its best because both sides bargained in good faith, so that small issues were kept under constant revision and did not become big issues at contract time. Years ago, strikes and lockouts were an integral part of free collective bargaining; but the main issues were big, and thus they had a far-reaching effect on all workers.
I believe that today strikes are outdated. Neither side can afford to strike, and if both sides bargain in good faith there is absolutely no need for a strike. Management must make a dollar in order to remain competitive, to pay the bills, replace worn out machinery and keep the plants up to date. At the same time, labour must realize that management has to borrow the money to pay salaries, even if sales are down in slack periods, and to expand plants in order to create more jobs. Both sides must work together if the business is going to be successful.
The former Minister of Labour was correct when he tried out the idea of labour specialists being involved in labour contract discussions. At least 60 days before a contract runs out, the government should force both sides to start meaningful talks on the terms of the new contract. At all these talks, a government labour expert should be in attendance. Sooner or later, regardless of the use of the strike, both sides will sit down and settle their differences, so why not do so before the contract runs out so that there will be no interruption of work? If both sides talk com-monsense there is absolutely no need for the strike.
Labour and management both have the same goals, namely to create a successful industry producing goods at the lowest possible cost. We must remember that it is the people who work who buy the majority of the goods produced. If industry had to depend on selling goods produced to management personnel, the same industry would starve to death. It is the little man who makes the wheels of industry turn by his constant buying of the goods produced. Any successful industry has been built on a combination of money and labour. One cannot work without the other; therefore, it is in the interests of all people to have industrial peace.
Is it not correct to say that the worker should share in the fruits of his labour by helping to make an industry successful? Is it not correct to say that he should be consulted when technological change takes place in his industry? All workers in all sections of our economy have a democratic right to expect fair, humane treatment and consideration for the many years of service they have contributed to helping industry become successful. In many cases, these same workers were the men who
Canada Labour Code
dropped the tools of industry in wartime and went away to fight for our democratic system so that it would not be destroyed. Surely they deserve every consideration when changes are to be made in industries. It is also correct to say that management has the right to expect a good return on their investment as well as the right to make changes in their plants so that they can remain competitive.
Each year many industries of this nation decide to make changes in their production methods. Some have decided to lock the door and to move to some other part of the world. The rapid pace of technological progress and economic growth can and does have adverse effects on the working population. If employees' resistance to change is to be less harmful, as it must be if Canada is to achieve its full potential as an industrial power, employers, trade unions and government must accept responsibility for the development and implementation of policies to cushion the impact of the change on individual workers. It is certainly not in the best interests of employers and residents of the communities affected to be saddled with the problems of relocating the employees without the help of the industry causing the shift through its technological plans.
When one looks at the railroad industry, one finds that since the introduction of the diesels thousands of once proud workers of the nation's railways have been dumped on the streets with nowhere to go. Today many of these workers have not recovered from the effects of this technological change. Canadian law should not permit this to happen. Many of these railway companies were given financial and other incentives to locate in various districts in Canada. Therefore, they have an obligation to provide service to the district in which they located in order to stabilize employment in the area. All these companies should be made to provide some type of compensation or retraining for their workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.
In this period of fast technological change, businessmen must have maximum freedom to employ new ideas and inventions that improve efficiency and keep their industry up-to-date. The workers affected by such change must have reasonable guarantees. When a machine wears out, it is thrown out on the scrap heap; but our human resources-the workers-have a responsibility to help us build a better society for all Canadians. Therefore, their future must be protected in such a way that society is rewarded by the work and ideas of the displaced worker. We must remember that these same new machines that displace workers do not buy homes, cars, furniture or the weekly groceries. They contribute nothing to our way of life other than to make man's labour less. At the same time they take away man's livelihood; also they pay no taxes or union dues.
Time and time again when there is a strike, management of large companies think up ways to eliminate jobs by the introduction of machines. They should have some responsibility to the area in which they locate to make certain that their former employees are retrained or relocated so that they do not wind up on welfare. There are far too many cases where our society as a whole is called upon to pick up man's broken dreams, desires and ambi-
1362

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
tions and try to piece them together. Surely, we must find some method of cushioning the shock of change.
I sincerely believe that the new Canada Labour Relations Board should be formed from public, labour and management personnel. Its full time members should have years of experience in their various fields, and there should be effective communication between them, the minister and his department, and all parties involved. I believe that, if the board is comprised of good, sound, experienced people, it can and will bring good industrial relations to all our labour problems so that decisions are made in the interests of the nation as a whole. Good industrial relations are based on an understanding of the problems involved. It is very important that the minister give the board the regulations which will help eliminate problems of management and labour and do not allow suspicion and hostility to creep in and slow down new methods of preserving industrial peace. I also believe that the extension of bargaining rights is a step in the right direction. For too long, many people in this group have found themselves in the area of no man's land and had to take what was handed to them with no hope of trying to help themselves.
As we move ahead into the 70's, we all have much to do to try to increase our production in a fiercely competitive world market so that employers can stay in business and give the working people of Canada the benefits of technological change, at the same time maintaining full employment. This is the challenge of the 1970's. Management and labour of this country can and must co-operate to help all Canadians build a greater country in which all of us may live.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, like my friends, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) and the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), I have worked in an industry that has been hard hit by technological change. We have all been affected financially by the results of the change and it is very hard to watch thousands of your fellow workers lose their jobs after many years of long and faithful service and be forced to try to build new lives for themselves and their families.
I sincerely hope that this legislation will help cushion the shock of workers losing their jobs in a fast changing society, so that all workers can be retrained and become productive members of our Canadian way of life and we can have industrial peace in Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill was introduced at a time when the Canadian people, especially the people of Quebec, can say that labour relations are not peaceful.
The preamble to Bill C-183 could lead us to believe that those who drafted this bill were really inspired by lofty principles. However, we know that given objectives are not always achieved, and the past has proved that though certain principles motivated the introduction of this bill, its application may be entirely different.
The measure introduced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) deals with several points. First of all, it deals

with the extension of collective bargaining. It also deals with the creation of labour relations board, with an erroneous definition of unfair practices, with the settlement of labour differences through the intervention of the minister as well as the procedures for the application of collective agreements.
Those are surely issues of current interest.
In addition, Bill C-183 provides a few amendments for the enforcement of the legislation when technological changes are involved.
Hereafter, an employer bound under a collective agreement who intends to make a technological change will have to give to the union a written notice 90 days before making it.
One can wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether a 90-day period will alter the present market for unsold products.
It is true that workers need a certain protection to guarantee their job and to avoid dismissal.
On the other hand, the manufacturer is compelled to make certain changes in his plant and to carry out new ideas, either to maintain his competitive position or to reach a high level of efficiency.
It is a well known fact that workers lie at the employer's mercy.
One must bear in mind that when a company or an industry is created, when industrialists decide to invest somewhere, it is not in order to provide work for people but simply to make money. We know that if it does not pay, it does not take long for them to scram.
We remember the poor work and pay conditions that labour experienced not so many years ago. And it is this situation which, in my view, has incited workers to unite in order to claim better conditions and pay.
In short, unions arose from a requirement. In my view, they will remain in several instances an essential instrument and way of protecting workers, as long as they are directed by leaders who are conscious of their responsibilities and the means used are sensible when it comes to remind some industry heads of their social responsibilities.
There have already been, and there can be more concrete results following negotiations when there is something to negotiate about. However, I see nothing in the bill likely to force a plant to remain open. And precisely because of closing down of operations, whether in the area of Montreal, of Trois-Rivieres, of Quebec City or of Saguenay-Lac Saint-Jean, it too often turns out that the worker must accept the status of unemployment.
Everyone is aware, for instance, of negotiations undertaken a few months ago, not to say a few years ago, and pursued by the CNTU on behalf of the "Lapalme boys". Now all the efforts of this union with Mr. Lapalme remained without result for the simple reason that Mr. Laplame, a former post office contractor, had just decided not to renew his contract.
Therefore no law can constrain businessmen to remain in business when it does not suit them.
April 17, 1972

And even though there is often a tendency to consider the employer as a big bad man, it should not be forgotten that he also has problems.
First he must keep up with technological change which requires considerable investments, and furthermore he must keep up with trends and major changes in the markets.
For the manufacturer, for the employer, another source of trouble is often the income tax. And it is not the least, Mr. Speaker, when one considers the income tax being paid by them.
Frankly, it is rather difficult for us to take a hard stand where the interests of some workers and some employers are concerned.
Industries able to provide work for hundreds of workers and with a turnover of several thousands of dollars are not always free of debt.
And even if powerful trusts do control such strong enterprises, we all know that some medium size industries, which play an important part in our economy, having been launched with very small capital investments, have managed to reach a certain level of prosperity and to obtain a fair share of the Canadian market. If those industries have managed to do that, it is simply through the great skill of their directors and also sustained and titanic efforts.
And it happens that the income tax act provides that such medium size industries shall pay their income tax before paying their debts.
In my opinion, such a procedure is absurd and as unfair as it is dangerous, since the survival of our employers in many cases is directly threatened by that bad tax system.
Under such a tax system, in allegedly prosperous years, our medium size industries can barely make it. It is useless for them to think of expanding or building reserves for bad days.
We all know that turnovers may vary greatly from year to year, especially in manufacturing.
We also know that the profit margin may vary. So, for a given year, the industrialist whose financial statement is fairly good has to pay a large amount in taxes, regardless of what his debts may be. If business changes for the worse he may even have a deficit and be compelled to borrow in order to remain in operation.
During rather good periods, the same person has often had to pay sizeable amounts in taxes. I know personally of the amounts paid by an industrialist who employs 75 people. The turnover increased thanks to the superhuman efforts of the workers under bad conditions. Despite everything, this man had, for three years, paid $25,000 per year in federal taxes.
But with a plant where everything had to be rebuilt, with an extremely small warehouse, he decided to borrow from the Industrial Development Bank in order to expand his undertaking. Today, he faces a changing market with a heavy financial burden and he is now wondering whether he should carry on his business or simply close down.
Canada Labour Code
Mr. Speaker, I think it is not normal that a manufacturer paying $75,000 to the federal government within a three-year period should have to face a $125,000 debt. In short, this man has to pay high interest on money he has already paid to the government. This is ridiculous.
I wonder if the present government, with all its experts, should not contemplate a system keeping in reserve the taxes paid up by manufacturers.
In case of real profits, the government should collect taxes and use that money to administer the affairs of the country. But this money, as I say, could remain the property of industrialists. A special account could be open for them so that they could use it whenever needed.
Thus the businessman who has allowed the government to use several thousands of dollars of his money over a number of years should also have the right to use this money whenever he needs it, and without any interest. Unfortunately, until now the tax has been strictly collected to serve only the government administration. Therefore, it seems to me time has come to think of something else.
The Canadian government, whose wish is to establish a just society, could establish a precedent in allowing industrialists to use this money, interest free; after all it is their own money that they have lent to the government during the years when their business was prosperous.
Mr. Speaker, if there are some bad businessmen, there are also a great many good ones who recognize their responsibilities towards their employees and who are also entitled to reasonable profits. The employee has always the right to live. Personally, as a member of Parliament, the majority of complaints I receive from ill-treated labourers are not coming from people who work in industries, whether small or large, but rather from federal government employees. In my view this is in striking contrast with the fourth paragraph of the preamble which reads as follows:
And Whereas the Parliament of Canada desires to continue and extend its support to labour and management in their co-operative efforts to develop good relations and constructive collective bargaining practices, and deems the development of good industrial relations to be in the best interests of Canada in ensuring a just share of the fruits of progress to all;
Mr. Speaker, this preamble simply states that the Canadian government desires to serve the genuine interests of the people by insuring that everyone gets a just share of the fruits of progress. It is somewhat unusual to read such statements in the preamble of a bill when this government does not hesitate to reclassify some of its workers to avoid paying them a salary increment. At this point, I will take the liberty of reading a letter I have received from the Quebec local of the Canadian Union of Transport Employees. It reads as follows:
Mr. Roland Godin M.P. for Portneuf Parliament Buildings Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
Some members of our local, which is a member of the M.D.O. group of the Quebec City airport, have submitted to us their grievances concerning the reclassification decided by the Department of Transport in respect of these employees.

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
In view of the present circumstances marked by an ever increasing cost of living, you will realize the confusion besetting these employees who are now faced with a salary decrease as a result of that reclassification.
We join them in their emphatic protest against a move we consider both unrealistic and inhumane.
These employees suffer the consequences of this reclassification with their hands tied up and can absolutely do nothing to offset the situation.
To alleviate this inequity, we suggest that section 7 of the Public Service Staff Relations Act be amended to enable the public service to negotiate the classification criteria by which we are now victimized through no fault of our own.
This letter is signed by the secretary of Local No. 10109.
Mr. Speaker, there is a marked difference between the bill preamble and what actually happens. Unfortunately, Department of Transport employees are not the only ones to complain since this juggling with the employees' classification is also taking place in the Department of National Health and Welfare.
For example, before integration in the Department of National Health, family allowances and old age security section in Quebec City, certain employees of the Department of Supply and Services which were working in Quebec City in the transfer unit were classified CR-2 with a yearly salary of $4,900 while those holding the same position in Toronto were classified CR-3 with a salary $1,000 higher.
This enabled the Quebec City office to have an administrative surplus of $107,000 for 1969-70; this amount was transferred to Toronto and allowed this office to pay the salaries I just mentioned.
It is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, but I must point out that this deplorable situation still exists in Quebec.
If the hon. Minister for National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) wants proof that the Quebec employees of his department are underpaid, let him read the duplicate of a grievance at the 4th stage signed by his deputy minister, Mr. Willard, which indicates that all positions in the family allowances units will be classified CR-3, starting June 1970. Even though the grievance settlement provides for a retroactive adjustment to June 1970, nothing has been done as yet.
Moreover, some hourly paid employees of the Quebec offices have not yet been appointed permanently and even after three years are still getting very low salaries and are deprived of all the benefits which they would otherwise enjoy.
As for the permanent employees here is what happened.
The employees held a well determined position, performed specific duties and were classified at level CR 3 whose numerical assessment was 424. One day the department decided to amalgamate all units into a single one, which meant that an employee who worked within a given unit-transfer, Indians, Eskimos, school attendance, maintenance and residence-had from then on to do the job of all those units, not to mention book-keeping. In order to do all this they had to get acquainted with the proceedings of all those units, which logically could only increase those five points used to assess a position: knowledge, complexity, consequences of errors, contact and

supervision. According to the national bureau that raised the numerical assessment from 424 to 434. Some time later the assessment of those people was raised from 434 to 441. Since the numerical code of a CR 3 varies between 324 and 450, that gave them the opportunity of reaching a higher level.
Now, what happened was that classification officers probably did their work half way, with their feet up on their desks, and finally assessed the new position at 401. Since the Public Service Alliance of Canada had classification officers who could do that work, employees at the Quebec office asked that the same positions be assessed, and precisely, the Public Service officer came up with a figure of 471, which would have allowed employees to be paid according to the scale and salaries in force in Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, this situation exists in Quebec. This is abnormal, and I think that since members of Parliament receive the same salary no matter what area of the country they live in, whether they come from Halifax, Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal or Quebec City, the Department of National Health and Welfare, which has to concern itself with and look after the welfare of every Canadian, should do its utmost in order to eradicate the difference of $1,000 between salaries paid in Toronto and Quebec City for the same duties.
Mr. Speaker, in this bill they even have the gall to talk of freedom, and clause 110, on page 7, reads as follows:
Every employee is free to join the trade union of his choice and to participate in its lawful activities.
But the word "freedom", Mr. Speaker, is a big word which has several uses. I can tell this House that it is a word which has a hollow ring, for instance, for Canadian National employees. If the individual is really free to do as he likes where unions are concerned, how is it then, that a section which appears in the small brochure on agreements published by the CN provides that unions and railway companies have to unite whenever it is necessary to sue a union member?
If the worker wants to sue his union or the railway, he already knows that he will have to fight both. So, he stands no chance of winning.
It has also been referred to "freedom" but this is a little untrue, as it is well known that today membership in a union is compulsory, at the risk of losing your job. Before the implementation of the Rand formula, this obligation did not exist.
I must say here that this is not true of all unions, because there are still some union leaders who work, but I say once more that in the case of our Canadian railways, the unions do not work so well.
And we have proof of this, for before the Rand formula was first implemented, railway employees were the fifth or sixth best paid Canadian workers. Since the formula became compulsory, as union leaders get their union dues whether they work or not, railway workers who again ranked sixth fell down to twenty-sixth position.
According to a federal government survey whose results were published recently, of $69 million in union
April 17, 1972

dues paid to unions whose central offices are located in the United States, $10 million represent a net profit remaining in that country. How is it, then that railway workers' union dues are increased without prior consu'ta-tion with them and that the railway companies subtract such dues from their pay cheques without asking for their consent? We know that railway employees paid $1 per month in union dues. A little later, in accordance with the Rand formula, those dues rose to $2.50, later still, they were $4.50 and now, in some cases, they are $7.50, $8 or $9. We know also that today the unions may even ask for $50 per month, and no worker can say anything about this.
Mr. Speaker, it is not surprising that railwaymen are always told: Ask your unions, they will pay for you. Such Canadian employees are in no position to plead their own case. When they attend an annual meeting for instance, they may be told: There will be a discussion on the internal administration of your local union. If you have complaints make them to the union headquarters in the United States.
In fact, at least 30 CNR employees sent letters of protest to their U.S. union headquarters in 1967 and they are still waiting for an answer. Such behaviour is far from being satisfactory.
I think we should recognize the right of workers to be consulted and to really share in decisions concerning their work and union contributions. I believe they should also be entitled to select their own representatives when negotiation time comes.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure there are many cases where the trade unionist cannot get the advantage of certain laws. He should also demand that the machine be at the service of man instead the other way around as it is being done nowadays.
Therefore, we should call for a thorough measure and not only a bill like the one now before us. This measure will be of value to very few people; it should be of a more general nature and universal in its application. Otherwise, it will boon be retrograde and will even become unjust before long.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding I should like to emphasize that the Canadian government really has a long way to go if it wants to be able to say that Canada is a place where life is worth living, a place where a worker may still chose his kind of work freely.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in many ways this bill seems to meet with general approval with regard to some aspects and considerations. I should like to confine my remarks largely to technological change which is the one area that has created considerable comment from industry, particularly as applied to the old bill. With the changes in the new bill, certain improvements seem to have been made.
While the bill seems to go a considerable way in meeting the objections of industry, it seems quite obvious that the passage of the bill will in the future create some difficulty in interpretation. It is quite difficult to define technological change. Many others changes occur that are allied to technological changes such as tariffs, delivery, wages, prices, depletion of resources and so on. These create
Canada Labour Code
conditions whereby change is necessary and cannot be disregarded, in spite of the situation in which industry or employees find themselves. In relation to technological changes and their effects, there is the very human social element of protecting an employee and his family who may suddenly find himself without a job as a result of technological changes beyond his control. In the new bill consideration has been given to the fact that the provision for a strike occurring during the life of a contract would act as an incentive for parties to include technological change provisions in a collective settlement.
The inclusion of the right to strike during the life of a union agreement, as has been suggested, causes other problems such as using the harrassment technique where the unions would threaten to appeal to the Canada Labour Relations Board on technical change provisions in order to get action on some other demand. It has also been suggested that it would cause many more negotiations, that is every innovation would require negotiation unless there were some very elaborate technological change provision in the contract beforehand. The Chamber of Commerce suggested that, in the face of increased industrial conflict, this would be an improved feature in the new bill. It has been suggested that objections to technological change would reduce benefits to everyone. This slower rate of change would be controlled by the labour union rather than by management. As was suggested, this would eventually mean increased costs and perhaps increased prices for consumers and would increase the risk in capital expenditure, ultimately driving up the price of the product in the economy.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give immediate consideration to the advisability of amending the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the pensions payable under these two acts to be available at age 60 to all persons who meet the other requirements of the said acts and are prepared to withdraw from the labour market, and also to provide for the basic amount of the pension payable under the Old Age Security Act, at age 60 for those not in the labour market and at age 65 for all others, to be increased to $150 per month, for this basic amount to be escalated each year by an amount that will enable pensioners to keep up with rising living costs and to share in rising living standards, and also for the elimination of any means or income test from the Old Age Security Act, so that the full pension thereunder will be recognized as the established right of all our people.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during the years that I have been in the House of Commons I have received many thousands of letters on the subject of pensions, the overwhelming majority of them approving of various proposals I have made. However, I must say that seldom have I had the volume of support that I have received in connection with this motion.
If my mail says anything, it says that the people of Canada are strongly in favour of improving our pension arrangements, and in particular they like and approve the idea of the necessary steps being taken so that those who wish may retire at age 60 and receive sufficient pension to make that retirement possible.
I know, Sir, the usual treatment that is given to private members' motions in this hour. They are usually talked out, sometimes with kindness and approval, but nevertheless they get talked out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext: You fare no better if they are passed. I had one passed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext:
The hon.
member says he had one passed, and fared no better. I suppose that is true. I have had many motions talked out, but I have had the pleasure of seeing the principles involved accepted a few years later. Even so I would hope that the House might consider this motion today as one that does represent the thinking of members in all parties, and the thinking of many Canadians, and that it might just let it come to a vote, might just let it pass and say to the government that the House of Commons would like the elements proposed in this motion to be given consideration.
There are, as will be clear to anyone who reads the motion, four basic elements to it. In the first place it asks for the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to be amended to make it possible for people to draw their pensions under those two pieces of legislation at age 60 if they leave or are out of the labour market.
The second element in the motion is one that calls for an increase in the amount of the pension to be paid under the Old Age Security Act. My suggestion is one that I have made quite a few times, and I shall stick with it until we win it. It is that the amount ought to be, as of now, not less
April 17, 1972

than $150 a month. I make the point that if we are going to take steps to permit people to retire age 60 then the amount of pension they will receive must have some form of adequacy or it will be meaningless just to give them the right to retire.
The third element in my motion relates to the escalation of pensions. For a while it did look as though we were moving ahead with the principle of escalating all pensions. We do it with respect to the pensions of retired public servants, retired RCMP personnel, retired Armed Forces personnel, retired members of parliament if they are over 60, and a few other groups. We also do it for those who are on the guaranteed income supplement. In their case the legislation still provides for an escalation of up to 2 per cent of the entire amount they are receiving. However, the government in December, 1970, brought in a piece of legislation that took away the escalation of the basic pension, which since that time has been fixed at $80 a month.
But this is a bit of digression which I ask to be regarded as part of my defining the third element in the motion which is to the effect that all pensions ought to have an escalator clause. In fact I think the rule should be established that a pension is not a pension if it is for a fixed amount for all time. There must be provisions for an escalator clause. We must also get to the point where we realize that escalation itself is without value unless it is realistic, unless it enables the pensioners concerned to keep up not only with the rising cost of living-and a two per cent increase when the cost of living goes up by five per cent is not good enough-but also with the rising standard of living. In my motion I put it in those terms by suggesting that there should be an annual escalation "by an amount that will enable pensioners to keep up with rising living costs and to share in rising living standards."
The fourth element in my motion is one that relates to the income, needs or means test that is applied to the guaranteed income supplement, which I feel should not be in the Old Age Security Act at all. I deal with this by asking for, "the elimination of any means or income test from the old Age Security Act, so that the full pension thereunder will be recognized as the established right of all our people." Let us pay the full pension universally, and let the income tax take it back from those who do not need it.
Sir, I feel that each of these four points is important. Perhaps in an immediate sense, thinking in terms of the persons who are on the pension at the present time, the most important is that the amount of the old age security pension be increased to $150 a month.
The other points, the escalation, and the removal of the means test are likewise of great importance. But I suppose I must say that if there is a reasonably new element in this motion it is the one that calls for lowering the eligible age. In the long run I think that is the most important one, for those who will be pensioners if this change is accepted, for those who will be pensioners in the future, and for our economy as a whole.
There was a day when work and the volume of work was such that retirement at age 65 was the accepted thing.
Proposed Pension Increases
I recall that many years ago when I started arguing and presenting private members' motions to reduce the eligible age from 70 to 65 some hon. members said that it was impossible. Even so, we finally got it down to age 65 for old age security. In the Canada Pension Plan we have the option that a person may draw benefit at age 65 or keep on working and contributing in the hope that the benefit might be larger by the time he reaches age 70. But, Mr. Speaker, the nature of work has changed and so has the philosophy of life. We have come to the realization that old age should not be just a few years when body and soul are held together until it is time for the graveyard; that it is a period of life in which old people, like young people, should have a chance to pursue their own interests, to do their own thing. If old age is to have any meaning in those terms it has to start while people are still capable of adapting to new ways of life. I suggest that 70 is old for that and so is 65-60 is a better age. If there is any criticism in the letters I receive, it is that retirement should start even younger than age 60, perhaps 55.

speechtext: Forty-five.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext:
I hear one of my 45-year old friends wanting it lower still. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in terms of the philosophy of life it is a sensible proposal to advocate voluntary retirement on pension at age 60. I emphasize the voluntary nature of this. Anyone who examines my motion carefully will see that I am suggesting that the one condition people must meet to come under the terms of the motion in addition to age, residence and so on, is that between the ages of 60 and 65 they are either out of the labour market or prepared to take themselves out of it.
As with the Canada Pension Plan I suggest that other income that one might have between ages 60 and 65, another pension, interest on investments, ownership of a house, and so on, should not count. These do not count now under the Canada Pension Plan between 65 and 70; the only thing that counts there is income from employment. I would like to have it that in both the Canada Pension Plan and under the Old Age Security Act, between the ages of 60 and 65 you can have all the other pension income you can garner, you can have various forms of income but the one thing you cannot have is income from employment and still expect to draw pension from either piece of legislation.
There is a fair amount of opinion to support the idea that there should be provision for a spouse who is under the age of 65 to receive the old age pension. This has been proposed in this House and I have supported it. I suggest this motion would take care of that to a considerable extent; perhaps it is all we need. In the usual case the husband is a little older and if he wants to work to age 65 when his wife is somewhere between 60 and 65, under this provision she could draw the pension without waiting until she reached 65. I think if hon. members will look at the motion as a whole they will realize that it meets the kind of situation that has been set out in this House a number of times and that we feel ought to be dealt with as soon as possible.
The other thing to be said and said very strongly on a proposal of this kind is that it is a way of doing something
1368

April 17, 1972
Proposed Pension Increases
about the unemployment problem that faces our young people. It seems a bit silly to keep the old man working past 60 and put younger people on grants to do something that can be thought up just to keep them from doing nothing. Why not pension the old man and let the young person have the job? I do not suggest this as a complete solution to the unemployment problem. The statistics I saw today suggest that there are just over 700,000 people in Canada between 60 and 65. I was not able to ascertain how many of those are in the work force, but bearing in mind that most unemployment is amongst the younger people there is a pretty good possibility that 250,000 to
300,000	of the 700,000 people between ages 60 and 65 are employed. I would guess that at least half of them, if they were given the opportunity to retire and draw the full old age security pension, particularly at $150 a month, and to draw their full Canada Pension Plan benefit and any other pension they might be entitled to from industry, would leave the labour force and take advantage of this proposal. I submit that we would create perhaps 150,000 or even 200,000 jobs. That does not completely solve the unemployment problem but it makes a bigger hole in it than I see in some of these press releases that come to our desks about the number of jobs created by certain departments of government.
I also point out that if you increase the purchasing power of the people over age 60, both those not now working and in effect those whom you retire, it would create a demand for more goods and services which in turn would create work and make a significant contribution to the solution of our present unemployment problem.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because this resolution makes such eminent good sense, because it expresses views I have heard expressed by members in all parts of this House, because there is such wide public support for it, I submit it to the House this afternoon in the hope that the House will indicate that it favours the elements of this resolution, particularly a lowering of the eligible age on a voluntary basis, increasing the amount of pension, putting the escalation on a realistic basis, and doing away with a means or income test so that the pensions our people receive when they retire will clearly be theirs as a matter of right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext: Would the hon. member concede that there might be some difficulty "for the elimination of any means or income test from the Old Age Security Act" because there is a fine line between a means or income test and retirement test under many circumstances. Would that not sometimes create difficulties of administration?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext: If the hon. member is asking my opinion, I do not think it would. This business of whether it is a means test, a needs or income test is a matter of definition. I would call what we now have a means test and my hon. friend would call it an income test. As for a retirement test, we already have one in the Canada Pension Plan and the administration of that plan has had plenty of experience in drawing the line between a means or income test and a retirement test. All I am suggesting between age 60 and age 65, in the case of either pension, is the retirement test, namely, that a person is out of the labour market.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Weatherhead (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to take part in the debate this afternoon on the notice of motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with respect to increasing pensions for senior citizens. I am especially happy to do so because this matter is of great concern in Metropolitan Toronto, the city I come from, and very important in Scarborough West, an area which has more than its share of senior citizens, being one of the oldest suburban areas of Metropolitan Toronto. Even though the government has considerably improved the lot of senior citizens in recent years, and rightly so, by introducing the guaranteed income supplement, which I believe now is at $137 for the senior single citizen, including old age security pension, and at $260 for senior citizen married couples, that supplement not being taxable as of January 1 this year, and even though the government increased income tax exemptions for single people to $1,500 and to $2,850 for married couples, the government has, for the first time, brought down an additional $650 exemption for senior citizens age 65 and over.

speechtext:
I am talking about the heavy involvement of the federal government in senior citizens housing. We supply most of the money for building senior citizens homes. We should not forget an area that, until recently, was the subject of much controversy, the area of medicare. Substantial benefits are available to senior citizens under our medicare program, and particularly to those in great need, for senior citizens probably need medicare more than any other group. This program is now fait accompli, and its accomplishment is now passing into history. Yet the medicare legislation was proclaimed less than four years ago.
However, as the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as well as others would no doubt say, much remains to be done for senior citizens of this country. They are the ones who made the country what it is. Before most of us were born, they went through the great war, they went through the great depression and, later, some of them went through the second world war. Some of us were around then. Those are the people who, during long decades, earned low and, in many cases, fixed incomes. Only in their later working years could they earn the greater incomes that our younger people have been able to obtain. Therefore, I think there is a good case to be made on their behalf, and the federal government should look on their circumstances with compassion.
I must confess that I am in sympathy with much of what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said about senior citizens. I am in sympathy with many of his philosophical ideas in many areas. Nevertheless, I am surprised that an hon. member who has been here for nearly 30 years can speak about increasing senior citizens' pensions without once mentioning how much those increased pensions would cost us. As I said, I am in sympathy with much the hon. member says. I work with him on committees and appreciate the great deal that he does. I also appreciate his strategy in what he is doing. Yet it seems strange, as I see it, that an hon. member can make a speech advocating substantial increases in pensions to certain senior citizens and advocating that the qualifying age be reduced to 60 for those not in the labour market, a change which might affect perhaps half our senior citizens, and not mention once, as I remember, the cost of this additional increase.

I confess I decided to speak about an hour ago and haven't had much chance to research my figures. I am willing to be corrected if my figures are wrong. Speaking from memory, I think there are about
1,700,000	senior citizens in this country at present; and of these about 1 million get either the whole of the guaran-
Proposed Pension Increases
teed income supplement or some part of it. About 700,000 senior citizens presently get the basic $80 per month. It seems to me that increasing the pensions of the 700,000 senior citizens who now get the $80 per month basic pension and no GIS to $150 a month would cost us nearly $600 million a year. I am talking about those who get their pension at age 65. Secondly, if you increased the pensions of the one million or so senior citizens who are getting the guaranteed income supplement, and, on average, they get about $120 a month, a figure which is pretty close, the expense would be about $360 million a year. Those are my rough calculation, increasing the pensions of people over 65 in the way the hon. member suggests would cost the taxpayers of this country approximately between $950 million and $1 billion a year. That is an additional cost.
However, that is not the end of the financial calculation, because the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has come up with an interesting and worthy idea for getting workers of 60 and 65 out of the work force. I do not think he suggests that this would solve the unemployment problem by any means. His idea I think is that if we could get about 150,000 senior citizens between 60 and 65 out of the work force, there would be more jobs for the younger people, the group with the highest unemployment rate. I think we ought to discuss this theory about whether people between 60 and 65 want to retire, and whether they are better off as retired people or as working people. There really is not much time this afternoon for me to go into this since others wish to speak on the motion.
Coming down to the financial end of it, and that is not the only consideration by any means, one can say several things. The hon. member has spoken about 700,000 people between 60 and 65 who are in the work force. I thought the figure was closer to 1 million; however I will accept the hon. member's figures since he has done some research and I have not had much chance to do any. Let us say that of these 700,000 people, half are out of the work force already. Of course, the half of those between 60 and 65 who are no longer in the work force include married women who once worked but no longer work, men who have retired early through sickness, company options, and that sort of thing. I think at least half of the
700,000	people the hon. member referred to are not in the work force.
If we do not entice any other people to leave the work force between the ages of 60 and 65,1 believe the additional cost of giving $150 a month would be roughly $630 million a year. Then, if we were successful in enticing a further 100,000 to leave the work force, the cost to the taxpayers would be an extra $180 million a year. I realize that what senior citizens are entitled to receive and what they deserve to receive is not a matter simply of dollars and cents, but it does seem to me there is need for a measure of financial responsibility even when we are talking about people for who we care so much. Unless hon. members can find some great fault in my admittedly rough arithmetic, I would suggest that the proposal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which would cost between $1.75 billion and $2 billion a year, would be a difficult burden for taxpayers to bear. I might remind the House that we have recently been discussing the idea of a

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext:
The hon. member refers in his motion to the basic amount being escalated each year by an amount which would enable pensioners to keep up with rising living costs and to share in rising living standards. Frankly, I cannot understand why this has not been done. I know there are some who would argue that the guaranteed income supplement has been increased by a large amount and that this increase is going to people who need it the most. It is said we cannot afford to give an annual increase to people drawing basic old age security pensions. I feel that most of the people drawing basic old age security pensions cannot by any means be considered to be wealthy even though they may have a little more than the ceiling established in connection with the guaranteed income supplement regulations.
It is true that there are a few E. P. Taylors about, a few wealthy people-lawyers, doctors, dentists and a few others who have made good investments and are still working in their late sixties and seventies-but these people by and large are paying high taxes anyway. If we gave them an extra 5 per cent or 6 per cent on their pensions, whatever the figure might be, we would get most of that money back by way of income tax in any event. For these reasons I believe it is essentially a phony argument to say that all those who are not receiving the guaranteed income supplement are well off. They may have a little more coming in than the others, income from a few stocks and bonds, but they are not well off. It would be much better, in my view, if we could give them a fair increase every year.
We all receive letters on this subject from retired schoolteachers and others who are now finding it difficult to get along on their pensions. My primary concern, of course, is for the people who have no extra income at all; for the two-thirds of our senior citizens who have no other source of money. At the same time, we should strive to make the old age security plan fair and meaningful and the best way of doing so,'while not bankrupting the treasury, is to make provision for reasonable increases each year in line with the actual increase in the cost of living.
One area in which we can increase pensions without placing too great an additional burden upon the treasury is that of the guaranteed income supplement. Senior citizens in receipt of these payments are now getting $137 a month, which is a lot more than they received a couple of years ago. But it is still well below the poverty line. Two senior citizens who are married and living together can possibly get by because their expenses can be shared, but single people especially are being asked to live well below the poverty line. I agree with the hon. member that these

senior citizens should be entitled to $150 a month rather than $137 a month as at present. If we were prepared to allow annual increases based on actual increases in the cost of living, we could go a long way toward giving this important part of our population its just due.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ambrose Hubert Peddle (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AMEND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN TO PROVIDE INCREASED AMOUNTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until half an hour or so ago I was not aware that this motion would be discussed today. I do not particularly wish to say anything in rebuttal of the contentions put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) or the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. It seems to me it would be very easy to say that the pension should be raised by a more or less arbitrary figure. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests $150 a month, and the hon. member across the way seems to agree with him. It would be an easy thing to say, "I think it should be $200 a month," but I would still be pulling an arbitrary figure out of the air.
I do not think a member of the opposition, in particular, should be expected to cite an appropriate figure. After all, the government has access to the work of various boards and commissions, including that of the Economic Council of Canada. The government has this expertise at its disposal and it should be able to arrive at a reasonable and practical figure at which the pension should start, tied to the cost of living, of course.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says the Old Age Security Act should be amended in order that people may draw pensions at the age of 60, provided they are willing to retire from the labour force. I see this as a means test in itself; at any rate, it is a string attached to the pension. I might say I am not at all convinced that these pensions should be granted without any strings being attached to them. I am willing to accept the government's word that the state cannot afford to provide a reasonable standard of living for everybody who reaches a certain age. While I agree that that is the ultimate, barring that I think the emphasis should be placed, as indeed it has to some extent, on those who are actually in need. Therefore, I do not agree that $150 is the magic figure, because it might be even more than that; I do not know. However, our pension provisions are due for an overhaul and the government should have those people who are expert in this field produce a reasonable, sensible starting point for a new pension scheme.
I subscribe wholeheartedly to escalation of pensions. I suspect that the reason various governments are not too receptive to this suggestion is that this would remove pension increases from the political arena. With pensions escalated on a regular basis tied to cost of living increases, no government in need of a few extra votes would in an election campaign be able to promise an increase in the old age pension. As I say, I subscribe 100 per cent to this suggestion, knowing that within the next year or so we will be forming the government. Even so, I do not think we would want to be subjected to this kind of temptation and this is why I endorse the proposal to remove it from the political sphere.
With regard to eliminating the means test, as I have indicated I do not think I could subscribe to this in light of
April 17, 1972

present conditions in our country. However, I do think that those with no means of support other than their pensions are entitled to at least a half reasonable living. The Economic Council of Canada has already drawn a poverty line, and although I do not recall the figure at the moment I suggest that this would be a good starting point for paying a pension to those with no other means of livelihood.
That would be over $150 a month.

If it is over $150 a month, I do not want to be arbitrary but it would seem to me that this is a decent, reasonable starting point without going into specifics. One aspect of pensions on which I welcome the opportunity to support the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre relates to those receiving the old age pension, having reached the age of 65, and supporting a wife. The hon. member referred to bringing a lady of 60 under the plan. I do not think this would go nearly far enough. For example, in my own part of the country terrible situations are caused where the wives of pensioners are aged 53, 54 and 55. There might be a few select areas in the country where a woman of this age can find gainful employment, but there are none in my part of the country and I suspect there are none in most other parts of the country.
If a man of 65 has a wife the same age, then together they draw a combined pension of $255 a month. However, living next door to them may be a male pensioner who has reached his sixty-fifth birthday and receives a pension but who has a wife of 55 who receives nothing, and although he has the same expenses he has to exist on $137 a month. From a common sense point of view, this is neither just nor decent. I think the government is beginning to recognize that when a man reaches this age he should be given the opportunity to live with certain dignity. I contend that the government should also give him the opportunity of discharging any other obligations he may have to his wife or members of the family who live with him. I support 100 per cent the hon. member's proposal in this regard.
To repeat, rather than pulling any arbitrary figure out of the air, I think the government should keep a close watch on this aspect. If the government pays any attention at all to this kind of debate, I think it should zero in on this problem and try to discharge its responsibility with a degree of common sense and justice. The family income security plan bill will be before the House again within a few days. This bill recognizes that the cost of living increases every so often, but even yet it has no escalation clause. At least, I do not think it has. However, when the bill becomes law it will triple family allowance payments in respect of children of some families.
I suggest the government should not only show great concern for one sector of society; it must show concern for all sectors. I think our old age pensioners are long overdue for further consideration and for a complete overhaul of their benefits. I suggest that those in government circles who read these debates should pay attention to the views expressed and give this situation the attention it deserves.
Proposed Pension Increases

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words, during the few minutes remaining before recess, in support of this motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
On many occasions already, the hon. member who has seriously examined this problem has submitted motions or bills for the purpose of either increasing the pension rates or lowering the statutory age for becoming eligible. Once again, I commend him for it.
I was very pleased earlier to hear him say that he favoured the payment of a pension to the spouse of the pensioner, even when the spouse has not yet reached the statutory age. Although the hon. member had not dealt with this problem in his motion, he insisted on saying a few words about it during his comments. I think I was, if not the first, at least one of the first to submit a motion in this respect to this House.
I note also that the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle) who spoke before me shares the same view.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest this matter is very important and it should be considered as early as possible.
The hon. parliamentary secretary who spoke after the member for Winnipeg North Centre said that after all the cost of such amendments to the Old Age Security Act would be prohibitive. In the Liberal Party, they think in terms of dollars rather than in terms of goods and services that can be offered to the people of Canada, and particularly to senior citizens.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, thanks to our means of production which are steadily developing, we could enable a great many people aged 60 or more to retire from the work force and still ensure enough production and services to all the Canadian people without depriving anyone.
This morning, I found on my desk a letter from a senior citizen who receives the old age security pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, or $137, starting this month. However, two persons have to live on this one pension; besides, both are seriously ill and it is a well known fact that drugs are tremendously expensive. These people have applied to the Quebec government for additional aid to enable them to pay for the drugs they have to buy every month. This was the reply: We are willing to pay any amount in excess of $30 a month for the purchase of drugs.
This situation, Mr. Speaker, is utterly ridiculous. This couple would have to spend $30 a month out of a total monthly allowance of $137 and would have to live on $107 a month. This is an all too frequent and unfortunate situation wherein pensioners have no choice but to live in poverty and misery. As a stopgap, they have to go without drugs in order to provide for other needs that are as essential as those of health.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that-as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre indicates in his motion-we do not have to pass that measure at once but rather to consider it. By the way, the parliamentary secretary himself

April 17, 1972

thought that it contained very important elements and he deplored that the government has not yet taken the appropriate steps. In fact, it seems to me that the cabinet should consider that situation as soon as possible in order to make the necessary changes.
Much could be said in every respect about the merits of this motion, but I wish to leave it to the House to reach a decision this evening on this bill. To conclude, I will support the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
