But that does not mean I am disillusioned with him or am not an admirer of his.
I think the words "give immediate consideration" are the hopeful words of this motion, but I must say my priorities are quite different to those of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I do not believe in the necessity of going back to the universal concept. I do not think the country could afford that. However, I do believe that basic old age pensions should be tied to the cost of living. I suggested a year and a half ago, when the minister first brought forward his aborted bill, that this was the situation. That bill was later withdrawn.
This matter involves the savings plans of all those who do not have a large income but whose income is enough to disqualify their receiving the benefit of the supplement. They should be paid a pension tied to the cost of living. It is the responsibility of the government to see that the cost of living does not go too high; and if it has to shell out from time to time because of an error, the people as a whole should have to pay, not just those who expect to have their basic retirement plans increased by $80. I am not capable of saying whether the country can afford to go higher than $137, but I think pressure should be maintained to go higher. Therefore, I think the government should be asked to consider, as the motion asks, whether or not we can go to $150 at this time for individuals.
Personally, I would rather see some other glaring errors corrected first. Somebody referred to married couples. I think it is a crime that some wives feel they are a drag on their pensioned husbands. Many of them cannot work because of health or lack of training, and it is a

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was detailing some of the problems of technological change in respect of this bill. I believe the technological change proposals must be criticized and assessed as a remedy to the problem. The problem is very simple but very difficult to rectify. The problem is to incorporate technological changes into Canadian industries so that they can compete with foreign industries in our domestic and foreign markets. At the same time we must minimize the adverse effects of such change upon members of the Canadian labour force, protect the public interest and carry out our public responsibility.
The present urgency in seeking solutions to this problem is twofold: the kinds of technological change Canada has experienced in the last decade or so have been introduced at a more rapid rate than in earlier years, and current technological change has a far reaching effect on Canada's manpower. The effect of technological change upon manpower requirements is diverse. It is generally associated with a substantial increase in the number of skilled, technical and professional occupations with a slower growth rate for the semi-skilled and unskilled occupational groups as well as among the Metis and Indian populations. I think this can be given as one of the reasons for the difficulty in respect of job placement.
Certain variables in the past few years have accentuated the effects of these trends. The rise in value of the Canadian dollar has made foreign competition more difficult to cope with and has led to a need for increased efficiency in production by Canadian firms. On the other hand, a very high level of unemployment prevents the reabsorption of displaced, semi-skilled and unskilled occupational groups into the labour force. Where Canadian industries have failed to take advantage of technological advance, labour lay-offs have resulted, one example of which is in the pulp and paper industry. Another problem of technological change is that it most often occurs in highly unionized industries.
The effects of accelerating technological change and a high level of unemployment upon highly unionized industries have contrit uted to uneasy industrial relations in Canada. Obviously, industry and unionized labour have an interest in technological change. It is equally obvious that the Canadian public has an interest. In the first place,
Canada Labour Code
the Canadian public is the beneficiary of an efficient and technologically competitive industry, or the financial victim of an inefficient industry that is protected by tariffs or bolstered by government subsidies. In the second place, taxes are variously used to assist industry to make technological changes or to assist employees to weather such changes. In the third place, the public has an interest as the victim inconvenienced by industrial strife arising out of management's and labour's failure to reach agreement on technological change.
The public, through its government, has an interest in technological change and its effects. This public interest is not one of convenience or inconvenience but of responsibility, because the public is responsible for the economic, fiscal, tax, tariff and trade policies of the government of the day. These policies may encourage or discourage an industry from making technological change, or encourage or discourage labour from co-operating in such changes. It is reasonable to assume that the public has a vested interest in the problems of technological change and, arising only from that interest, the right and responsibility to be a third presence, with management and trade unions, in contributing to the solution of such problems.
One area which is clearly difficult to define is what is meant by technological change. It is obvious that where a new machine displaces workers, this will be a technological change. However, there are many other areas where technological change will not be so obvious. Therefore, I think there will be a major problem in defining technological change. There is also the provision that a significant number of employees will be affected. In a large concern there may be quite a number; in a small concern it will be as great in number in relation to the total working force. This in itself is an element of discrimination. It is just as important a matter for one employee who is displaced by technological change as it is for 100 workers who are being displaced. One of the interesting developments that may occur with technological change is whether or not the stability of the long-term collective agreement will be maintained because strikes are possible in mid-contract. There seems to be general agreement that the long-term contract has been beneficial to management, labour and the labour union. These matters will have to be resolved in the future.
Any discussion about the effect of this technological change clause and its actual working mechanism must, I believe, be considered in light of what the country will need in the way of new jobs. In the very interesting survey conducted by the Science Council of Canada, entitled "Technology in a Cold Climate," it appears that we in Canada have promoted and encouraged a large amount of skilled labour and highly trained people but we do not yet have the technological industries to employ them. Canada is faced with the urgent problem of creating a large number of new jobs in the 1970s. However, our industrial production has been disappointing. Canada's index of industrial production rose by 3.1 per cent in 1971, compared with 2.1 per cent in 1970. During the last decade, the sixties, the growth factor was 6.4 per cent. Therefore, the 3.1 per cent figure of last year is disappointing compared with the sixties. Manufacturing production increased, in

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
volume terms, by 2.3 per cent compared with a decline of about 1 per cent in 1970. There has been in recent years relatively slow growth in industrial production, even with the pick-up of industrial and manufacturing production in the 1970s.
In the April 14 edition of the Globe and Mail there is an article headed "Exports to U.S. offset reductions elsewhere". The article points out that the first three months of this year showed a substantial drop compared with Japan, the European Economic Community and Great Britain. Without the increase in exports to the United States our trade position would be in dire straits. What does this mean? Our increase in trade with the United States was composed largely of crude petroleum, natural gas and lumber-both renewable and non-renewable products. We have been questioning whether we should export these materials in large quantities.
This technological change provision will be very important for the balance of the seventies. Statistics indicate that the peak of entry into the labour force has passed. Last year the labour force growth rate was 3.1 per cent, and total population growth was roughly half that. As the projections of the Economic Council show, the role of the labour force will in fact be slowly diminishing in relation to the rate increase. However, it will still be among the fastest of any industrialized country.
The impact of technological change has a dual role. We as a nation desire technological change because, presumably, only in this way will we make any changes to increase our productivity, create new jobs and achieve a sustained standard of living for our citizens. However, as far as the individual worker is concerned, in many cases technological change will mean only disruption of his way of life and he will become understandably unhappy with his situation.
As far as the effect of technological change is concerned, and notwithstanding the clause in this bill, I think it will greatly depend on the situation at the moment. If there is not high unemployment, it is likely that technological change will be accepted with minor effect. Increased employment benefits, severance pay, and so on, should take some of the sting out of these changes, but if unemployment remains high technological change may well become a bone of contention.
The bill affects two important groups of federal employees about whom I am concerned both from the point of view of my constituency and western Canada in general. This bill affects railway and transportation workers employed in grain handling and grain elevators, industries under federal jurisdiction. There are many ways in which changes have affected employees and communities without, perhaps, falling directly into the area of technological change. Technological changes will make a vast difference to grain handling, railroading, the agricultural structure and, ultimately, social and rural life in western Canada.
For a long time there have been rumours and suggestions that wholesale changes in our grain handling system will be necessary. Although the grain transportation committee has made a report, the minister in charge of the wheat board has not yet seen fit to divulge its contents to the public. However, enough seems to be filtering out of

the secrecy adopted by the government to indicate that the report will contain a somewhat centralized grain delivery system. This will mean the phasing out of many smaller elevator points throughout western Canada. Those employees under federal jurisdiction will be affected.
With the abandonment of the branch line protection by 1975, many railways in western Canada will be abandoned. Weeds will grow along the tracks. In my own area, the possible abandonment of a whole subdivision between Dauphin and Hudson Bay junction, via Swan River will cause significant changes in the whole agricultural economy. Many of the proposed changes do not seem to make sense. I urge the minister in charge of the Wheat Board to make public the report on grain handling as soon as possible so that we can begin discussion on the merits and demerits of the proposed changes. The technological changes that will be present in the rationalization of grain handling and its effects on railroading and the agricultural economy will be enormous. The value of grain production in western Canada has not changed in the past 20 years. This means that the increased costs of transportation will have to be met out of greatly reduced income. The provisions regarding technological change might well be too hasty or premature in the areas of grain handling and railroading.
If there is any doubt about the effects of technological change that will be forthcoming affecting transportation workers and, in particular, railway workers and other employees involved in grain handling, no clearer indication need be noted than that a senior official of the CNR in western Canada has said that the time will shortly come when present rates for the transportation of grain will not be sufficient to sustain the flow of locomotives and boxcars necessary to meet the needs of the grain industry. I think the request by the CPR that the federal government assist in the leasing of American diesels and boxcars to move grain to the east indicates the future trend. There will be a request for an increase in transportation charges with respect to grain. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we will see an attempt made to have the Crows-nest Pass freight rates set aside.
Coupled with so-called rationalization of the grain transportation industry there will be widespread technological changes which will affect the employment of many railroad workers and of elevator workers both at inland terminals and local elevator systems. How this bill will help with respect to technological changes remains to be seen.
The government seems to have made some reasonable changes compared with the provisions of the original bill. Obviously, it should be an advantage that during negotiation of a new contract an employer will be able to bargain with a union on the laying down of guidelines for technological change. This should go some way toward preventing strikes.
So far as the grain handlers are concerned, I point out that a situation exists in Vancouver where the handlers have been working without a contract since last November 30. Should a strike be called by their union, it could well be disastrous. This bill can have an important effect
April 17, 1972

on transportation and grain handling and in committee I will be interested to hear the views of expert witnesses on this aspect of the problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to concentrate my brief remarks on one aspect of this proposed legislation, that part of it which, as the case may be, has to do or has not to do with the fishermen of Canada and, more particularly, their status in regard to collective bargaining. This is a very important issue in the part of the country from which I come, as it is important in other parts of Canada.
My colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), who is our spokesman on these matters has already voiced several of the opinions which I am about to put forward. I am sure that following his return to Ottawa this evening from the west coast, he will again be on his feet either in this chamber or in the committee proposing amendments to improve the legislation.
Last week I was glad to learn from the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) that he is quite willing and indeed would be happy if representatives of the British Columbia fishermen, through their organization the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union of British Columbia, appeared before the committee which will be discussing this legislation in detail. I know, as the minister pointed out, that this is a matter strictly within the purview of the committee; it alone can decide what witnesses to call. But I think Canadian fishermen must be encouraged to know that the minister has no objection to their representations being placed forcefully before the committee. I believe it is important that this be done.
To put the matter briefly, Mr. Speaker, the fishermen in British Columbia contend that the legislation as drafted could deny collective bargaining rights to a majority of the fishermen of the country. Surely this should not be the case. The fishermen of Canada are working people; they should not be denied the rights of working people. As drafted, the bill proposes to include some fishermen within the definition of "employee" in the Canada Labour Code, but unless the present wording is amended it could exclude a great many fishermen, indeed the majority of British Columbia salmon fishermen who have been organized and have bargained collectively since 1893.
The exclusion of fishermen who are employed on their own small boats, fishing for large processing companies, contradicts in the first place the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in 1956 which deemed all fishermen to be employees within the meaning of the act. In the second place, it contradicts the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act and section 411 of the Criminal Code which granted all fishermen in British Columbia equal exemption with all other workmen from the anticombines provisions of the legislation. Thirdly, it contradicts the recommendations of the Woods task force which proposed that all fishermen who are economically dependent for the sale of their product on a very limited market be given collective bargaining rights.
The provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland recently amended their legislation in order to provide collective bargaining rights for fishermen. Formerly their legislation excluded inshore fishermen who used their
Canada Labour Code
own small boats. The amended legislation included all fishermen. It is upsetting to find that the legislation which we are discussing tonight has been drafted in such a way that a great number of Canadian fishermen could be denied collective bargaining rights.
Judge Nathan Green, industrial inquiry commissioner, stated in 1970 that the co-adventurer principle is an "unrealistic, outmoded idea which has no relevance in this day and age to this type of operation." The artificial division of fishermen, by legislation, into employee fishermen and self-employed fishermen is unrealistic and outmoded. It deprives thousands of Canadians of basic rights already available to most citizens.
Again, we find indications that the government plans to remove the majority of commercial fishermen from enjoying the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The term "self-employed," if it were applied to all fishermen working on their own small boats could effectively be used to exclude a considerable number of fishermen in British Columbia from UIC protection. All fishermen in Canada were covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am sure they wish to continue to be covered by it. The situation reminds me of an old slogan first used many years ago in a campaign in British Columbia to secure coverage for fishermen under the Workmen's Compensation Act of that province: "Fishermen are workmen in fact. Why not under the Unemployment Insurance Act?" One might add-"and the Canada Labour Code?"
From the point of view of fishermen, probably the most important change they would seek in this bill is one providing basic equality for all fishermen. They need a more adequate and all-inclusive clause defining fishermen as employees. I am not a member of the fisheries and forestry committee nor the labour, manpower and immigration committee, but I suggest a definition along the following lines:
A fisherman shall be deemed to be an employee under this act. Fisherman means a person engaged in commercial fishing in waters under the jurisdiction of the federal Department of Fisheries or on the high seas, accepting or receiving payment according to the volume and price of fish caught and delivered to an operator who purchases fish, regardless of whether such fisherman (a) owns and operates his own fishing vessel (provided he as master-owner of a fishing vessel does not employ or engage more than two additional fishermen who share in the proceeds of the fishing voyages); (b) shares in the operation of a fishing vessel owned by another person and receives in payment for his services a share or portion of the proceeds of the fishing voyages; (c) operates a fishing vessel owned by another person under a rental agreement or conditional sale agreement or any other form of oral or written agreement or (d) receives wages for all or part of his employment on a fishing vessel or in fitting out a fishing vessel on which he will be employed.
I think the intention should be to make sure that all fishermen engaged in commercial fishing on smalle " boats are included whether or not they be owners of the small boats on which they are employed. At the same time, I would propose to exclude from the category of employee those vessel owners who employ more than two men on their vessels. That would really mean that the master-owner of a fishing vessel who employs three or

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
more crew members would not be classified as an employee.
Mr. Speaker, I urge the minister and the members of this House, particularly those who are or will be members of the committee to which this legislation will shortly proceed, to harken to the voice of the fishermen and make definite provision for their spokesmen to appear before the committee and explain the difficulties involved in this legislation which will handicap them in their earning capacity through collective bargaining. This will give the spokesmen an opportunity to present the type of amendments, changes or improvements which they seek in the legislation in order to protect themselves.
This is a matter of very grave concern to many thousands of workers on the seas and, incidentally, to their families. The Minister of Labour has so far indicated a fairness of mind and of procedure to a greater extent than some of his predecessors. I am told that the minister believes or has said that the position of the fishermen in this matter is basically unassailable. I, too, believe that it is unassailable and that my few remarks tonight should be taken as some indication of the view of the fishermen, particularly those of British Columbia and, I am sure, of other parts of the country. I conclude by saying that I am sure the committee to which this legislation will be sent will give full consideration to the protection of the workers in one of our basic industries.

Mr. Speaker, first I should like to say how gratified I think most members on this side of the House are that both the official opposition and the other opposition parties have expressed support for this measure. I think we have come to the realization in this country that the rate of change in society, the rate of change in industry makes mandatory the introduction of measures to assure that the price of technological change is not going to be borne by the working people with countless tragedies province by province.
We know that there has been substantial change in the nature of industrial development, especially in the last ten years, and that people who up to this time regarded themselves as beyond any possibility of unemployment are now being rendered unemployed, not because of some fault of their own or because they have been found to be inefficient but because new machines have been invented. The revolution of automation and cybernation is sweeping this country as it is many other countries. We are now told that a man will hold at least three different occupations during his working life.

Technology is not only affecting the man who works at the lathe, in the shipyard or the auto assembly plant; it is affecting those in the executive suite. Some people in this country who are today criticizing this measure-and I do not think they fully understand Bill C-183- will perhaps find themselves in an economically insecure position in a few years. We are told by the Economic Council of Canada that at any given time 3.8 per cent of the work force will be seeking employment even during times of technical full employment. This is why since 1968 the government has introduced such a wide range of measures including those designed to provide temporary income support through the new unemployment insurance program, new working opportunities through the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and why this winter, for example, the special employment program will see almost $500 million invested by the government in providing jobs for 150,000 Canadians who would not otherwise have work.
The government is quite properly and deeply concerned with the whole matter of the technological revolution. The present law, which we are really seeking to change, has not been changed since 1948. The section dealing with technological change has been given a great amount of publicity, yet misunderstandings remain.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext: Then why did you change it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
In recent months I have met with groups in different parts of Canada. I have visited Halifax, Nova Scotia and I have spoken on Vancouver Island, and at points between. There are still some people who believe they are somehow going to be affected by this bill which proposes to provide a measure of protection for those affected adversely by technological change. A funeral director in Ontario contacted the department and said that he felt this proposed measure would cripple his intention to introduce technological change in his operation. But, of course, the profession of mortician is not within federal jurisdiction. This measure applies to industries within federal jurisdiction. There are people who say that may well be true, but when a law like this is brought in at the federal level some provincial government is going to pick it up and bring in a similar measure.
I submit this measure is a good one and we should get it into committee where we can make modifications. If it can be demonstrated that these modifications would improve the legislation, we should make them; and if the legislation is good, it should and will be imitated by the provinces. If it is a bad measure, if this is bad law, then of course it should not be emulated in other jurisdictions.
Surely we in this House day after day receive tragic letters from those who have been displaced in jobs as a result of automation or new technology. We hear of economic tragedies which occur in all provinces from British Columbia to Newfoundland. We have a responsibility, in
April 17, 1972

so far as it lies within our ability to act at the federal level to make sure that these tragedies do not take place.
We propose that the terms of this proposed law shall not apply to collective agreements which contain provisions designed to cushion the impact of change. Happily, progressive companies in this nation have entered into contracts which make provision, in some cases, for the impact of change. In my province, British Columbia-a highly unionized province-many leading companies have brought in the kind of provision in contract agreements that we seek to bring in under federal jurisdiction.
Of course, these clauses of the bill do not apply in cases where there are provisions in the collective agreement for the negotiation and settlement of problems arising from technological change and where notice in writing of the change was given during the open period of a contract. The technological change provisions would not apply to existing collective agreements, but only to those made after the bill comes into force. The pertinent sections have also been modified, so that when an employer gives notice of a change during the open period this notice will not be invalidated because he is unable to give precise information as to the likely effects of the future change.
Hopefully, when the bill is studied in committee we shall hear from various groups of this country. I assure the hon. member who spoke previously that representatives of the fishermen will be invited to come before the committee to submit their case. I have met with them, as has the hon. member. They have raised persuasive arguments in some areas. We should not enter the committee hearings with dogmatic views. We should enter the hearings with the absolute determination and concern that is necessary if the legislation is to meet the needs of the workers of this country.

Mr. Speaker, arguments advocating that we do these things always interest me. It seems to me that there is some correlation between our having one of the highest standards of living in the world-

speechtext:
-and one of the most productive work forces of the world, and our having lived under free, collective bargaining up to this time. Our present economic difficulties do not lessen my basic confidence in the free collective bargaining process. It is too simplistic to suggest that if we could just get tough with labour, or just get tough with management, we could remove all the inconvenience and hardship that is caused by certain lockouts and strikes. That sort of argument is one of deceptive simplicity because any government that accepted it would soon be resented both by labour and management. If any government bureaucracy were established to bring about compulsory settlements and to take punitive action against those who failed to obey, the government setting
Canada Labour Code
up such bureaucracy would soon meet the resentment of both labour and management.
Some people talk in terms of labour courts. Have they really studied that proposition? More work days are lost in Australia, where there are labour courts, than in Canada. For years we have heard about the mature relationship between labour and management in Sweden. I have been to Sweden, as have many in this House, and I think it is a most impressive country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
What happened in Sweden last year? There was inflation of 10 per cent and a breakdown in the so-called mature relationship between labour and management. So far they have been able to negotiate and consult as to how large wage increases should be in Sweden, and they have arrived at a percentage applying to various industries. There appears to be no hard and fast method for conducting labour-management relations and no method whereby difficulties may be totally removed. During recent months, as some hon. members may know, there was a massive walkout of workers in Sweden and the Social Democrat government of that country had to order a return to work through compulsory, government edict. That Social Democrat government did not want to take that action. It had to do so because the situation was such that economic problems far more serious threatened to ensue.
I suggest that free collective bargaining is the best method of conducting labour-management relations in the North American context, Mr. Speaker. It might not be right for other countries. It certainly is right for this country. Since we have achieved so much through the free collective bargaining process down through the years, the government is determined to make the system work better. It is no accident that since the introduction of the industry specialist concept in Canada there has been a dramatic reduction in the number of work days lost through strikes and lockouts in this country. There were 132 man-days lost per 10,000 man-workdays in 1968. For last year the figure way eight days lost.
The whole key to Bill C-183 is this: it seeks to remove all those factors that apart from monetary factors lead to deterioration in labour-management relations. It seeks to remove the bricks of misunderstanding that arise during the life of an agreement-and during the open period labour and management can talk about monetary matters and economic issues. One of the basic causes of labour-management discontent in this country has surely been the festering sores which develop during the life of a contract. Some of this misunderstanding arises from fear of economic insecurity.
With new technology spreading throughout the world and affecting everybody's job, people are concerned. They want to know if they will hold their job next year. That is one of the misunderstandings we must remove if we can. That is why the technological change provision is included in the bill. That is also why, to the disappointment of some Canadians who really have not thought the matter out, the bill does not contain proposals for the arbitrary settlement of labour-management disputes.

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
There are certain situations in which the public interest is so clearly being affected adversely that governments must act directly. But, Mr. Speaker, these situations must be so extraordinary that we deal with them on an ad hoc basis with the method which appears to be most effective at the time. If through some extraordinary circumstance a government of Canada, be it this or any future government, should decide that the Parliament of Canada here assembled must vote on a certain matter affecting the public interest, that government should take its chances at the polls and let the people decide whether its action was truly in the public interest.
The bill before us, an act to amend the Canada Labour Code, is just one in a series of measures designed to help the Canadian worker. We have had the first major overhaul of the Unemployment Insurance Act since its inception 30 years ago. We have encountered some problems since the introduction of universality on January 1 but there has been a dramatic decline in the number of complaints received, and members of all parties who voted for this bill are finding their judgment confirmed that they voted well.
The Canada Labour (Standards) Code increased the minimum wage ot $1.75 and gave the governor in council power to enact further increases. It provided for maternity leave, strengthened provisions concerning equal pay for similar work, prohibited dismissal for reason of garnishment, provided for advance notice when employment is terminated and made provision for severance pay. These and other measures are complementary to the measure now before us. Each one is designed to remedy the irritations, the misunderstanding and the economic insecurity which had led to a deterioration of labour-management relations in some jurisdictions of this country.
The transitional benefit program protecting workers affected by the automotive pact has been extended to July 3, 1971, for application and to July 3, 1974, for benefits. We are extending the industry specialist concept in order to promote meaningful communication between employers and employees and to attach more importance to preventive mediation. This initiative has resulted in early settlements of disputes in such industries as railways, airlines, longshoring, and so on.
This is the pattern of government legislation, to make sure that in this highly competitive world not only will companies be encouraged to introduce useful technological change, so that Canada may compete successfully, but to ensure that there is a minimum of misunderstanding and disruption in labour-management relations. I hope this measure will be referred to the committee as quickly as possible. I have appreciated the opportunity to speak tonight. I know that members from all parts of the House will attend those committee meetings in a constructive spirit determined to improve, if possible the bill we have before us.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make some general comments about the bill before us. I wish to refer to a group of people in our society to whom little reference has been made during our discussion as to the effect of Bill C-183. The measure deals

mainly with two groups in our society, labour on the one hand and management on the other. Each of these groups is well organized.
The labour unions made their appearance many years ago and gained considerable power during the depression years. They continued to work for the benefit of wage-earners generally and it is undeniable that they have improved their lot over the years. In doing so, they have acted responsibly and by and large have won the respect of Canadians. Today the unions make up one of the most powerful forces in our economic society. Although, as I say, they have won the respect of the majority of the people because in the main their actions have been responsible and just, there are some today who feel that the unions have become too strong and that they are no longer acting responsibly. I suppose it depends which way you look at it, whether this criticism appears justified or not. The fear is expressed, too, that the voice of the small man is no longer being heard in the labour movement; that the small man is being increasingly dictated to by those at the top, often from beyond our borders. So much for one of the groups we are talking about in this debate.
Opposing the unions is, of course, management. Management varies from ownership or control of small businesses employing very few people to the corporate giants, the great companies which have grown to their present position through continued expansion or through amalgamation with other corporations. In any event, they now wield tremendous economic power. Not only can they expect this power as individual companies, but many of them are banded together to form what is known as the Canadian Manufacturers Association. So we find these two great groups confronting one another.
This seems to be an age of confrontation, an age of war. The ultimate weapon used in this confrontation, is, of course, the strike. Strikes sometimes lead to violence, something we deplore and which can certainly bring no benefit in the long run to anyone. In extreme instances the right of the mob takes over. It appears that today any person with a cause or a campaign believes he is entitled to use violence to achieve his ends. Someone said it is the divine right of the mob to use violence. Canadian society deplores this; it can only lead to destruction of property, and so on.
The Canada Labour (Standards) Code, built up through the work of successive parliaments, has served as a means of modifying the effect of clashes between two great forces in our society. It also seeks to devise ways and means to prevent labour disputes reaching the strike stage, much less the violent stage. The bill before us is a further landmark on the road to better labour relations. It is the outcome, as we know, of the Woods task force study and embodies many of the recommendations made by that task force. When we get to the committee stage, we on this side of the House will be suggesting further provisions which we believe should be included in the legislation. As the previous speaker said, there appears to be general agreement on all sides of the House that the major proposals contained in Bill C-183 are acceptable.
The thrust of my remarks this evening, however, is not directed to the two groups I have mentioned, groups which are sufficiently well organized to enable them to
April 17, 1972

look after themselves: I am more concerned with the silent majority-the silent, unorganized majority, as it might be called-within our country; the suffering public, if you like. These are the people who were inconvenienced by the strike of postal workers, a dispute which affected everyone in the land. These are the people who are caught up in the confrontation between government and public service employees in Toronto where garbage collectors have walked off the job. The citizens of Toronto are suffering the effects. At this moment a general strike is gripping the province of Quebec; it is causing untold hardship, much of which is felt by ordinary citizens who have no means of rectifying the situation.
I have called this third group an unorganized majority despite the fact that some people might argue that their interests are represented by the Canadian Association of Consumers. Nevertheless, it appears to me that the consumers association is a somewhat loose and voluntary organization which does not pack sufficient punch to be of real effect when situations of the magnitude I have been describing take place.
It is estimated that the labour force in this country numbers about 8,500,000, of whom only one-third are organized. The total population of the country numbers roughly 21 million. So hon. members will understand what I mean when I say that the vast majority of Canadians are obliged to sit on the sidelines as silent spectators to watch the giants grapple in the ring of labour conflict. And they are the people who are hurt.
Where does responsibility lie to protect the people in general from the damage being done to them? Surely the two antagonists have some responsibility-management and labour both. They must act responsibly and see the consequences of the demands that they make one upon the other. Just as surely, government has a serious responsibility to protect the people whom we in this House of Commons as members of parliament represent. It is our responsibility to speak up and to take the steps that will prevent the silent majority from being hurt in the way they often are. I think we agree that Bill C-183 is an attempt to do this.
There are some suggestions I should like to make to the minister which can be explored in committee during examination of this bill and which will help to mitigate the suffering about which I have been speaking. I suggest that when we come to discuss division II and section 111 which make provision for the new Canada Labour Relations Board the government will be appointing, perhaps an amendment should be moved to provide that one or maybe two representatives on that board be from consumer groups in this country. They should be persons not involved in labour or management organizations on either side but, preferably, persons who have to live on fixed incomes or on a pension. I seriously suggest to the minister that some thought be given to letting these people have a voice on the board so they can bring some sense of perspective to demands being made during negotiations.
How do we avoid labour chaos? The Financial Post has some suggestions on how to avoid labour chaos, and I
Canada Labour Code
should like to take an opportunity of putting them on record. The Financial Post for April 1 had this to say:
This week's general strike by nearly all public servants in Quebec once again underlines the urgency of new moves to stabilize labour relations in the public sector. It should be obvious by now that bargaining in the public service has been working badly and is deteriorating. Federal civil servants each time they are asked, vote in growing numbers to use bargaining machinery that includes the strike rather than alternative machinery that ends in arbitration. What's to be done? Some realistic ideas have been put forward in Quebec by the Conseil du Patronat, a broadly representative employer federation. The conseil would have essential services defined clearly in law and it would have stiff penalties for those who violate this law.
This is always a stumbling block, I submit, Mr. Speaker. What is an essential service? No person in this country can agree on that, so the suggestion here is that it be clearly defined in law, with stiff penalties for those who violate this law. The article continues:
It would also insist that no strike in the public service take place until the union and the employer have agreed how essential services will be provided. If they cannot agree, some public agency should decide for them.
Perhaps that is something the committee can work out in its study of this bill. Speaking to the Rotary Club in the town of Simcoe not too long ago, a labour relations expert from Hamilton made some suggestions which might be helpful to the committee in regard to trying to reach a peaceful settlement of this thorny problem. Among other things he said this:
The public must be shown that they will benefit from an industrial climate that is not impeded by long, costly and unjustifiable strikes.
He expressed opposition to compulsory arbitration, which he said has eroded the decision-making process and led to buck-passing, especially in police, fire and hospital employee disputes.
Instead, he advocated legislation giving government industrial relations agencies the power to take steps to avert strikes and to act quickly in advance of crises.
He proposed the new laws should provide for ministerial or legislative intervention, and open the way to a variety of procedures. A fact-finding board appointed by the Minister of Labour would be useful in effecting settlements.
Some of these suggestions are now new, but I think we should take another look at them. What I have been saying is that a great portion of our population gets hurt without having any way to defend itself. Some people have referred to it as a ploy, a jockeying for position and power between labour and management verging on what might be termed brinkmanship. I should like to put on the record a quotation from the Gazette for April 12. The writer of this editorial pretty well sums up what I have been trying to say, in these terms:
A strike is similar in some respects to war. It may be just, although a just strike is as hard to define as a just war. It is a question of causes, objectives and alternatives.
In no case does a strike settle the question as to who was right and who was wrong, however these terms may be understood. Reasonable arguments do not decide the issue. In a strike, as in war, superior force and staying power win out.
In other words, it is the little man who suffers. This quotation points out rather dramatically, I think, the crisis in labour-management relations. I hope that when the bill gets to committee in the very near future those who are charged with responsibility for studying it at length, with listening to the evidence that will be presented by various

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
groups in society, will pay heed to what is said. Members of parliament, as representatives of the overwhelming number of innocent people in this land, have a very heavy responsibility in this regard. The bill must be discussed and studied logically. Political expediency should be put into the background. The government side of the House should be ready to listen to reasonable proposals which we of the opposition are ready to present and which we feel are just and fair. Members of parliament must see to it that the majority of the Canadian people are protected from the unfair and unjust effects of prolonged strikes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Steven Otto (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister oi Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no particular objection to this bill. It is a nice little bill. I am not going to put too much blame on the minister at the present time, since he took over the bill from his predecessor, but I am wondering whether the government and the bureaucracy which had a great deal to do with the bill are really looking at the facts of today's situation.
Reading the preamble to the bill, it speaks of "promoting the common well-being through the encouragement of free collective bargaining," "labour-management relations," "support to labour and management in their cooperative efforts to develop good relations and constructive collective bargaining," and so on. A short while ago I heard the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Perrault) speak of this concept of labour-management dispute, and hon. gentlemen opposite in their speeches continue to say what a nice little bill this is and similarly talk about labour-management dispute. If hon. gentlemen were talking about the circumstances that existed 30 or 40 years ago, then I would agree. However, I would suggest that there is no such thing today as labour-management dispute; there is only labour-consumer dispute or, indeed, labour versus labour in another field.
When was the last time an hon. member here obtained evidence of an entrepreneur taking a profit cut because of a strike? An entrepreneur may be in difficulties after a short time, depending upon his contracts, but in the past 15 years or more any increase in wages has been passed on to the consumer. We are talking about the preamble to this bill and the bill itself as though we were dealing with a set of circumstances surrounding a strike by organized labour when it originated 100 years ago, when money was locked into a certain community or nation. Money is not locked in today; it is a fluid thing.
If, indeed, there were such a thing as a labour-management dispute, and if there were some method by which management could be forced into absorbing a demand for an increase in wages, a great deal of investment money would have remained in the United States. Why do you think almost 38 per cent of the European economic market is owned by U.S. interests? That was the place they could get more productivity with cheaper labour. They could get this in Japan, and they put money in Japan. Consequently, for the last number of years there has been no such thing as a labour-management dispute. These disputes have been strictly labour attempting to

obtain an advantage for itself at the expense of the consumer and that is the fact.
Let us consider the question of strikes which is referred to throughout the bill and its preamble. I have no particular objection to the section about technology, because industry will absorb that and has nothing to fear from it. It does not matter how great a problem labour becomes, prices will be increased. Since every segment of industry is organized today, you cannot control this and you cannot say one entrepreneur will be able to do better than another because they are all in the same boat and are faced with the same unions and organizations.
What happens today is that a strike, the principle of which was developed long ago, is of no benefit to the labourer, the union man or the nation. Obviously, a strike is of no benefit to the country. The parliamentary secretary said there was always a .8 per cent loss; in other words, eight days lost per 1,000 days of labour-management dispute. I venture to suggest that those figures are based only on direct strikes. I attempted to find out about the other reactions in respect of people who could not work because of a strike in a certain industry but there was no record of it.
I inquired about the results on productivity per month before and a month after a strike, but found there are no figures. I know from personal knowledge and from what friends have told me that before a strike is entered into when there is no contract, production keeps dropping until about a week before the strike. A firm is lucky to have 10 per cent production at such a time. After a strike is settled no one is really happy. Certainly labour is not happy. Therefore, there is a gradual increase in productivity. It starts very slowly and takes at least a month before reaching maximum productivity. Therefore, everyone loses in the process.
I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that in reality what happens throughout the nation as a result of a work stoppage is a reduction in productivity which in turn causes an increase in the price of goods. Perhaps the price increase does not occur for four, six or ten months, but it certainly does eventually.
I think it is wrong to suggest that we still have labour-management disputes. These disputes are really between labour segments in different capacities. This is what is disenchanting to our nation today. This is why we have a demand from various centres for wage and price controls.
The hon. gentleman opposite who just concluded his speech spoke about compulsory arbitration. I put it to him that compulsory arbitration will not work, because even when you get the people back to work there is no way you can guarantee productivity. The people can be back at work, drawing wages, while at the same time productivity can be dropping. These people can work to rule, as experience has shown, and productivity is not immediately recovered. It is inconceivable that everyone will be happy with any sort of compulsory arbitration. There will always be those who are dissatisfied. The same thing applies to wage and price controls. I discount these two methods as feasible alternatives to what we now have.
Just for a moment I should like to review what I meant when I said a strike today has really no effect on industry.
April 17, 1972

A strike is a bad thing for the nation and it is bad for unions and organized labour. Let us consider what happens when there is a strike or a work stoppage. As I indicated to a union meeting I addressed five or six years ago, during the term of that particular strike the employees would lose in the neighbourhood of $1,180 in wages. That was based on a pretty good guess of the length of the strike. I also anticipated the settlement, and I was very close. The strike lasted 42 days. The employees received the increase they wanted, but they had to dig into their savings to make up for the loss of $1,180. It took them 2j years with the new increase to make up that loss. This sort of thing has occurred over and over again. Labour does not profit from a strike. Indeed, this is what George Meany was talking about. I recall that the leader of the NDP (Mr. Lewis) said exactly the same thing in Montreal two years ago. A work stoppage does not benefit labour at all; it penalizes labour.
This bill should be attempting to solve the problems of today. It should be an adventurous bill facing the realities of strikes and containing methods of putting an end to work stoppage as a means of settling disputes. It is work stoppage that really causes harm. I think one might suggest that work stoppage is the cause of the inflationary spiral we are suffering. If an industry does not produce, it must lose, because it has to pay wages. One of the things this government must face immediately is how we can adopt alternatives to methods we now have to prevent work stoppages.
I disagree with those who suggest that unions have no place in our society. The requirements of the past have not changed; the only purpose of a company is to make money at any price. Having been involved in business, I am the first to admit that business today does not display any sort of social conscience. Perhaps this is because of the general structure of business with its one purpose, that of making money. If it were possible for an enterprise to do so it would operate as a labour baron of 50 years ago, so the unions do have their place.
I should like to see this bill containing provisions requiring every industry to be organized. It is not fair that 60 per cent of the work force should not be organized while 35 per cent or 37 per cent is organized. If we accept the idea that there is nothing wrong with organization-and I accept it-we should all be organized.
The problem we face is the work stoppage. I believe we are mature enough to realize that in business when there is a strike there is a carrying on of expenditures, and so on, and the company does not make much money. Suppose we had a situation where there was no contract or where a contract had come to an end, and in lieu of management and labour taking practical positions and trying to outdo each other the company continued in operation, the employees continued to work and the profits made during the period until there was a new contract went to the government as 100 per cent taxes. The industry could not complain, because it would be better off than if it were on strike. On the other hand, how long would the shareholders support a corporation which declared no profit, because a strike might continue for a long period?
Canada Labour Code
If production continues, the working man is better off because he does not have to dip into his savings, and the government and the nation are better off because there will not be any loss in the gross national product. Business will be better off in reality because at least there will be greater incentive to negotiate a contract. How long can it retain the shareholders' confidence if it does not declare a profit?
Then there is the question of whether or not union dues would be paid to the government. I am not suggesting this is the only way to handle the situation, but the prevailing thought in this government's mind should be how to solve these problems without work stoppages. Every unionized man has the same problem. He has perhaps gone through a strike five or six times and realizes he is no better off today than he was ten years ago. Most people in this country feel there is something wrong with labour-management disputes since they receive no benefit and industry receives no benefit. On the other hand, we lose productivity and ground to other nations which have solved or partially solved this problem.
So I see no great difficulty in accepting the technological change section of this bill. I think industry will absorb it and I do not believe there will be the rash of strikes which has been suggested. If the government is at all aware of this problem, it should know there is something wrong with its whole technology in respect of settling disputes. I suggest this bill should have been as dramatic as the criminal reform legislation in which the government took a position that was audacious and realistic. At that time we had the nerve and guts to put in the Criminal Code amendments which meant something and which the people wanted.
I think the same urgency prevails within the structure of our labour-management or labour-consumer difficulties. The government must face the issue and make up its mind whether it intends to introduce price and wage controls which will not work, introduce arbitrary or compulsory arbitration which is doubtful, or bring in other provisions by which all of us in Canada will be better off and through which we will not have to suffer work stoppages time after time, an old weapon which has become useless. I think this is the issue which should be covered in the bill. I cannot see anything here to indicate that the government has faced the problem which should not be allowed to continue if anyone is to benefit.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by and large the bill before us deals with people working under federal jurisdiction for whom the basic right of collective bargaining is generally accepted. The bill has certain proposals which the proposer of the bill and indeed many commentators have agreed go some distance toward improving that basic right.
My main purpose in rising to speak is to deal with one group of workers in this country for whom the basic right of collective bargaining has not yet been established and satisfied. I refer to the commercial fishermen. I believe there has been previous discussion of this subject during the debate, but I should like to add a few thoughts. It seems to me that when one considers the situation of the commercial fishermen and working people in this country, one really must go back to something more basic than

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
the existing labour act or the labour code. One must in the federal field think, among other things, of the Combines Investigation Act. Members who are familiar with that legislation will recall it has in it a section which provides that nothing in the act shall be so construed as to deny workmen and employees the right of free association for the purpose of collective bargaining.
In my view that is the Canadian embodiment in statute of something for which workers fought and for which some workers died over the years in the United Kingdom and elsewhere, namely, basic recognition of the fact that when workers get together for purposes of collectively dealing with their basic rights of working, the kind of conditions and remuneration they should receive as a result of their labours, it shall not be construed to be a conspiracy, seditious or otherwise. This principle really has not yet been given statutory recognition in Canada in respect of the commercial fishermen who harvest the resources of our seas, lakes and rivers.
This, I believe, is a basic fact in respect of the situation in Canada which should be stated in connection with the approach we are taking to this bill. It is true there is some reference in the bill to fishermen. I believe I am right in saying this is the first time there has been such reference in federal labour legislation to fishermen per se. Fishermen, in the sense that we ordinarily know them, people who go out and work their own boats and gear to fish, or at least a segment of them are referred to under the definition section of the bill as "dependent contractors". The bill states that a fisherman who is not employed by an employer but who is a party to a contract, oral or in writing, is a dependent contractor if he is engaged in a joint venture with other like persons. The bill does not include a fisherman who goes out as a single person with his own individual tools of work, in his own small vessel and engages in a fishery.
Under the definition of employee, the bill says that a dependent contractor for the purposes of this act is an employee and, therefore, is entitled to the collective bargaining rights that other employees have under the proposed legislation. I suppose one could say, so far so good. But the fact remains that the bill as drafted excludes large segments of people who are really engaged in identical work under identical kinds of contracts, at least in principle, oral or written, who happen to be conducting a solo operation. If the legislation stays in this fashion, I suggest we are simply going to compound an already confused situation.
I would like to draw to the attention of hon. members a definition of "fisherman" for collective bargaining that was proposed in a bill introduced in one of the legislative assemblies of Canada. It was introduced into the House of Assembly of the province of Newfoundland. This matter may already have been referred to by other members. In the definition section of that bill it says that "fisherman" means a self-employed commercial person. It is very simple and straightforward. It goes on to provide:
-(including a sharesman or person agreeing to accept in payment for his services a share or portion of the proceeds or profits of a fishing venture, with or without other remuneration) engaged in fishing for gain, other than for sport-
I quote this legislation to show that there is a very significant contrast between the definition in the bill before us, and in my view a very important question of principle is involved. The bill which was introduced into the House of Assembly of the province of Newfoundland
begins as follows:
"Fisherman" means a self-employed commercial fisherman ... not falling within the definition of employee in the Labour Relations Act-
It specifically makes clear that it also includes a sharesman who is engaged with one or more other persons on a boat. It seems that the deficiency in the definition in the bill placed before us by the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) becomes very apparent when one contrasts the definition section in the legislation of Newfoundland with the proposed clause in Bill C-183. This includes only those who are together in a venture; presumably-I interpret this from my reading of it-two or more persons. I think the ridiculousness of that situation is apparent at once to anyone who has any familiarity with the practices followed in the fishing industry. In some cases there is one person on a boat, in some cases two and in some cases five or six. In other types of operation there may be eight or ten people on a boat, all engaged in essentially the same operation of catching fish and disposing of them.
The question has often been raised whether such people can properly be considered to be employees in any sense of the word. I am sure the Minister of Labour and the former minister of labour, now the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey), who I note is in the House this evening, are aware that there are some organizations in this country which are still arguing that point, stating directly their opposition to the acceptance of the idea.
I understand that a brief was submitted to the former minister of labour by the Fisheries Council of Canada. At least the copy sent to me so suggests. It states quite clearly that in their view they made a mistake when they did not go to court over the issue of fishermen being considered employees for purposes of the Unemployment Insurance Act. We had quite a long debate, at the time, on the question of including fishermen in the act. This was finally included in a government proposal and became operative. That, of course, was the subject matter of another debate not very long ago when we were revising the Unemployment Insurance Act. The suggestion in the brief of the fisheries council that even if a fisherman is an employee, he is not an employee within federal jurisdiction, is another argument. I think that illustrates the complications of the situation in which we are involved.
Hon. members may recall that this matter came up not long ago in relation to certain developments in the province of Nova Scotia. The suggestion was made that if a ruling were to be arrived at as to which jurisdiction fishermen came under, the minister of labour of the federal government and of the province should declare in advance that they would be prepared to introduce the kind of legislation which would ensure proper collective bargaining rights for fishermen. Without attempting to go into all the learned argumentation in that particular case, I think it is sufficient to point out that there appears to be a growing body of evidence that many learned judges in

April 17, 1972

this land believe the concept of fishermen as co-adventurers is outmoded and out of date in this day and age.
Sometimes we are inclined to think that those who sit in high places on the judicial benches of this land are up in the clouds. But from time to time it is most refreshing to see, from the kind of recommendations and suggestions that come from the bench, that some of the judges in the high courts are very much aware of the realities of the developments taking place within our country. One of the realities of the situation in Canada today is that for all practical purposes a commercial fisherman is within the grasp of a large corporation just as much as is a logger, a worker in an automobile plant or a worker in any one of a dozen other industrial activities that one could mention.
It is a fact that in the province of British Columbia the market available to an individual commercial fisherman by and large is in the hands of two large corporations, commonly referred to as the Big Two. To the best of my knowledge one is the wholly-owned subsidiary of an American concern and the other is part of the Weston empire. It may be surprising to some hon. members to learn that the name Weston, usually associated with biscuits, plays a major role in the financial holdings controlling the buying and processing of fish on both the Pacific and the Atlantic coast.
I suggest that since this bill does take a timid step in recognizing the facts of the situation, that fishermen for practical purposes are employees, the minister should go the whole way before the bill proceeds further. I do not know how optimistic one can be about that, but I do know that according to a press release issued by the president of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union in British Columbia on February 25, 1972, it was stated that the Minister of Labour said he believed the union had presented an unassailable case for extending proposed legislative amendments so as to provide bargaining rights for all commercial fishermen. The emphasis there must be on the words "for all commercial fishermen." I hope that before we conclude this stage of the debate the minister will be inclined to make that statement official if indeed he did give that impression, which apparently he did, to the president of that fishermen's union.
However, if the bill passes second reading and is considered by the committee, I am sure the minister must realize that this whole question will be the subject of considerable discussion and debate. Certainly some members of this House are quite determined that that kind of clarification should be made so that all commercial fishermen will be equal in status.
Mr. Speaker, this whole question has been left up in the air so long that I am a bit like the fisherman who when there is a little nibble says, "Let us make it a good, big catch while we are at it." I remember when the whole question of collective bargaining for fish prices in British Columbia was put in jeopardy under the Combines Investigation Act. As I recall it, that was in 1956 or 1957. As the minister well knows, an amendment was made which was passed for one year specifically exempting this process only on the British Columbia coast and not on the Atlantic coast. It was just for the British Columbia fishermen.
Canada Labour Code
That happened to be the place where collective bargaining was well established, with a tradition going back for many years.
That particular amendment, which I regard as an extension of the basic provision that is in the Combines Investigation Act, namely, that nothing in that act shall be so construed as to prevent workmen or employees from getting together to bargain in respect of wages and working conditions, covered a small segment of the fishermen of Canada. When I say "small," I do not want to indicate that it was not a very important segment. The decision was made to meet a problem which was faced by a good proportion of the fishermen of British Columbia. But under that umbrella it did not take in fishermen anywhere else in Canada, whether on the Atlantic coast or inland. That particular act was repassed year after year for quite a time, until finally it got into our statute books in its present form and it will remain in effect until it is repealed or a group of ten members introduces a resolution calling for its withdrawal.
This brings me back to the matter of the Newfoundland legislation. I cannot say that I am fully informed on it, but as I understand it the Newfoundland legislation has been passed but not proclaimed. It is suggested that because the limitations of the existing federal exempting sections of the Criminal Code and the Combines Investigation Act apply only to the British Columbia situation, this complication under the Combines Investigation Act potentially still exists for all the fishermen of Atlantic Canada.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the suggestion made by a judge in Nova Scotia to my mind really means that the logical thing to do to avoid this mix-up is for this parliament to pass legislation including all of them; and if some of the other provinces take similar steps then hopefully by some rational approach, either by a reference to the Supreme Court or otherwise, the situation can be clarified as to where exactly the constitutional jurisdiction lies.
As far as I am concerned there is no excuse for our sitting back. By and large, it has been a fact of life in Canada-it is certainly true in the province of British Columbia-that the only governmental body that shows active concern for the commercial fishermen is the federal government. A joint commission was set up in British Columbia in 1964 to study price and wage disputes in the fishing industry of that province. A report was made, but nothing has happened as a result of it. I cite that as an example of the fact that if this parliament waits for appropriate action by the provincial government, the position of the fishermen will remain for a long time in iife present unhappy state of uncertainty in some parts of the country. They have already endured this unhappy situation for too long; in fact, I have been amazed at their patience.
If it were not for the fact that in some situations the fishermen are being treated as employees, even though under the legislation ordinarily applicable they are not, they might be satisfied to deal, in terms of bargaining collectively, under the umbrella and safeguard of the Combines Act if it were generally applicable. The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure the Minister of

April 17, 1972
Canada Labour Code
Labour is aware of this, that there has been a long series of court actions in British Columbia, where the nub of the matter is that the fishermen involved have been assessed substantial damages for certain action taken by them in connection with disputes, on the ground that they did not abide by the labour act of that province. In other words, they did not have the right, because they were not a trade union in this situation, to picket. This question has gone all the way to the court of appeal. The voluminous document in my hand is a copy of the argument in that case. This may not be the end of it because in due course it may find its way to the Supreme Court of Canada.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this case makes a strong argument, if we are to have any rationale in the fishing industry and if there is any hope of arriving at a situation where we will not have the unhappy events that surrounded this case which led to court action, for this federal legislation to provide the foundation for collective bargaining rights for all the fishermen of Canada. If it should be challenged in the courts and if the arguments advanced by some parties are correct in the view of the Supreme Court, at least the fishermen will know where they have to go. If they cannot come to this parliament for collective bargaining legislation, they will know it is a matter they will have to deal with through their provincial legislatures. It may well be that a determination will be arrived at which will make it clear that there must be legislation in both the federal and provincial fields in order to protect all commercial fishermen under the umbrella of ordinary labour law.
I would suggest to the minister that no useful purpose will be served by keeping the bill as it is, making workers of some fishermen and something else of others. At least the federal legislation should be clearcut and precise. From my reading of it, I would suggest that the kind of definition section which is in the Newfoundland bill would cover the question as far as making clear that all commercial fishermen are to be deemed to be employees when they are in the kind of relationship that commercial fishermen are in with respect to the buyers of their products.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I realize the legislation before us generally represents the work of many people over a period of time. I welcome some of the steps forward that are contained in it and I know some of my colleagues have discussed them in more detail. I should like to say, however, that I am glad we have this opportunity of a full-dress consideration of changes in the Canada Labour Code. It is certainly a much more useful contribution, to put it mildly, than the burden of amendments to labour legislation that we had a few years ago which, in the view of some of us, emasculated the Canada Labour Relations Board. To the extent there has been that kind of change, I should like to offer a word of praise.
