maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-SETTLEMENT OF CONTRACTS ON REGIONAL BASIS
PUBLIC SERVICE-SETTLEMENT OF CONTRACTS ON REGIONAL BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 24 I had an opportunity to put a question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) about settlement of contracts on a regional basis. I
recognize that I am not the first member of parliament to raise this issue; it is one that has been accelerating since 1967 when the government led bv Right Hon. Lester Pearson established a formula for negotiating settlements of contracts on a regional basis. I think that probably Parliament suffers from all the regionalism that it can stand.
I have tried, in my time here, to eschew adopting a regional stance on every issue. However, this is an issue that affects particularly public servants in the Atlantic provinces and it is my duty to remind the House again of the unfairness of the government's stance in this regard. The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), at page 1037 of Hansard raised the issue and questioned the anomaly of the settlement of contracts on a regional basis on the one hand and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion's trying to do its best to equalize conditions of pay, opportunity and so on, across the country on the other hand.
I felt that the parliamentary secretary on that occasion left a good many things unsaid in his answer. He seemed to relate regional pay with the mobility of the public servant involved. I suggest that that surely cannot be the only criterion for regional pay scales. For example, I cannot for a moment imagine the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) accepting the principle that judges of the supreme or district courts of, say, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick or Nova Scotia should receive less pay than those of Ontario. Those learned gentlemen are by no means mobile; they cannot be expected to move from one part of Canada to another.
One finds the problem of regionalism and lower pay scales prevalent in the nursing profession. I am speaking of women who are in the public service, who are serving at Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals across the country and who are receiving different pay for doing exactly the same work. Mr. Speaker, I put it to you, this is manifestly unfair of the government. This practice has been creeping into wage settlements, if I can put it that way, and I think it is time to warn the government that those who represent areas that will be affected particularly by the unevenness of wage settlements will be pressing the government to reverse a policy that can only work hardship on public servants.
I think the government is obligated to set the highest possible standard as an employer, and it fails in its obligation if in the bargaining process it uses the fact that, unhappily, incomes in one part of our country are substantially below the national average. I suggest, with great
April 17, 1972

respect, that it is time the government took another look at this policy. It is not in the national interest to proceed further with settling contracts on a regional basis.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Clermont (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-SETTLEMENT OF CONTRACTS ON REGIONAL BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Treasury Board's position with respect to regional rates of pay is certainly not an attempt to institutionalize a dilemma of regional disadvantages and disparities. As indicated by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) when the hon. member first raised this question, the regional pay rate system is in fact "an attempt to bring about, in an orderly way, a greater measure of unity".
As employer, the government is committed to paying rates which are equitable and competitive with rates being paid outside the public service for similar occupations. Where the outside pay data for occupational groups indicate significant variations from the Canadian average and where the area of recruitment and the mobility of employees within the public service is limited, the government as employer considers it appropriate to pay regional and not national rates of pay. Paying national rates of pay in such circumstances would serve only to overpay employees in some regions and to underpay employees in other regions in relation to the rates of pay prevailing in those regions. Neither situation, from the employer's point of view, is desirable or viable. In order to avoid this situation, regional rates are considered more appropriate.
The hon. member expressed the belief that the regional pay system is an attempt to institutionalize regional disparities. As the hon. member is aware, the basic objective of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is precisely to facilitate the access of people to productive employment opportunities. If the effect of regional economic growth is to raise rates of compensation in areas of low pay by comparison with other parts of this country, the government as employer will ensure that its rates reflect those changes, subject of course to collective bargaining provisions in the public service.

maintopic: POLLUTION-GREAT LAKES-UNITED STATES VETO OF SEWAGE DISPOSAL PROJECTS-EFFECT ON JOINT PROGRAM
POLLUTION-GREAT LAKES-UNITED STATES VETO OF SEWAGE DISPOSAL PROJECTS-EFFECT ON JOINT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 17,1 asked the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) the following question:
In view of recent reports that the proposed $138 million anti-pollution program for an accelerated clean-up of the Great Lakes has been vetoed by the Nixon administration, I wish to ask the minister what effect this decision will have on the joint Canada-United States program to deal with this problem.
I followed with a supplementary question in which I asked the minister whether the veto by the Nixon administration meant that the target date of 1975 for meeting certain standards would need to be revised. In his reply the minister said he felt Canada and the United States would agree in principle on a clean-up program and that he hoped the date of 1975 need not be revised.
Since I asked that question, the Great Lakes water quality agreement has been signed. I attended the signing ceremony on April 15, 1972, and I must admit, frankly, I feel it is a step forward. I am certain it will be welcomed

by most individuals in this House and by interested organizations across the country. I must point out, however, that the terms of previous treaties have not been observed by either country. In particular, I would draw attention to the Boundary Waters Treaty Act which was signed in 1910 by the United States and, at that time, by Great Britain. This treaty prohibited the pollution of the Great Lakes by any means or in any manner. It seems to me it would be much better had the two parties who signed the agreement last Saturday undertaken to carry out the terms of the original treaty, because I believe that treaty to be far more inclusive than the agreement which was signed on Saturday.
Conclusion of the agreement on Saturday does not ensure that adequate standards of water quality will either be made or set. In fact, there is every indication that inadequate standards are already being considered. The governor of one of the states bordering the Great Lakes stated yesterday that the standards being considered with respect to phosphates, fluorides, mercury, etc., would not ensure the success of the clean-up operation required. I agree. There is every indication that a very wide difference of opinion exists between Canada and the United States as to the standards required if an appropriate clean-up job is to be carried out. A good example of this difference is clearly outlined in the approach taken by our two countries to the problem of phosphates. We have sharply curtailed the amount of phosphates allowed in detergents used in Canada. On the other hand, the United States has not done so.
A very interesting article appeared in the Vancouver Sun tor April 15 in connection with a statement made by representative Henry S. Reuss of the United States. The article reads as follows:
Henry S. Reuss said today that the U.S.-Canada Great Lakes anti-pollution pact was a victory for the phosphate deterent industry and a potential disaster for Lake Erie-
Canada was put in the position today of signing the agreement, which lacks a ban on heavy phosphate detergents, "or having no agreement at all".
Reuss said a joint U.S.-Canadian study released in February showed that if phosphates continue to be dumped into Lake Erie for the next few years there is the "frightening possibility" of the "irreversible destruction of the lake".
My point is that this agreement talks of a 50 per cent reduction in phosphates, and I say that is not enough. Last August the federal government and the government of the province of Ontario signed an agreement to spend $250 million, I believe it was, on construction of sewage disposal plants. One pollutant they were aiming at was phosphates. We have already on our statute books legislation providing for a sharp curtailment of phosphates used in detergents. Yet we are faced with the possibility of a job being done on one side without a full or proper job being done on the other.
I should also like to point out that this agreement is not a firm commitment or a treaty but merely an executive agreement set out in very broad terms. It does not tie the United States down to any timetable, or Canada either. It is merely an agreement between the two countries which acknowledges that a very undesirable condition exists in

I mentioned earlier that I was a little disturbed at the lack of action on the part of the United States over the past three years in regard to cleaning up this great body of water. Only two months ago the Nixon administration vetoed a $138 million program which was to have been the initial start of this clean-up project. It seems to me that we in Canada must push very strongly and do everything we possibly can to persuade our counterparts across the line to get on with the job. I am convinced that high international standards must be set and that these must be policed and enforced by the International Joint Commission if we are to get the job done. This is what I urge upon the minister.

speechtext:
I should like to amplify the response given on March 17 by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) to a question by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding). The inquiry concerned reports that a decision has been taken within the United States administration not to proceed with a group of particular projects for water quality in the Great Lakes basin costing in total $138 million, the largest item reported as being for studies on programs to overcome pollution from storm sewer overflows.
Naturally, we always like to see additional financial and other resources for sound projects to correct sources of pollution on the United States side of the Great Lakes, particularly where such pollution might have a transboundary effect on Canadian waters. We have made inquiries in Washington about this particular group of projects. We have been assured that the decision taken by the administration in regard to these projects will not have any significant effect on the broader programs to abate and control pollution in the Great Lakes which are incorporated in the agreement signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and President Nixon on Saturday last, April 15.
In this context I should like to draw the attention of the House to current estimates of the cost of programs to abate municipal pollution on the United States side of the Great Lakes as announced by the responsible agencies of the United States administration. The United States environmental protection agency has recently estimated that to construct the needed improvements to these municipal plants on the United States side will cost about $2 billion in total, over 31 years. Under agreements for sharing these costs proposed by the United States administration, about one half of this total would be provided in the form of federal grants with the remainder financed by state and local sources.
The flow of United States federal funds to construct municipal sewage treatment plants has recently increased significantly. According to reports issued by the environmental protection agency in Washington, federal United States government grants for the construction of municipal treatment facilities across the country increased from about $215 million in 1969 to $1 billion in 1971. For 1972 and the following two years the President has proposed increasing the flow of these grants to $2 billion annually, or a total of $6 billion for the three years. Of these grants, a substantial portion is expected to be directed toward the construction of needed sewage treatment facilities on the United States side of the Great Lakes basin which, as I have noted, is estimated to require expenditures of about $2 billion in total in order to meet tne terms ot tne new agreement.
I wish to assure the hon. member that it is the intention of this government to carry out the programs envisaged by the recent agreement and we have every reason to believe that our United States counterparts intend to do likewise.
